items.excerpt: Arshan Najafi‘s Zenosyne takes its title from John Koenig’s neologism describing the unsettling sensation that time seems to accelerate as we grow older. items.body: Arshan Najafi‘s Zenosyne takes its title from John Koenig’s neologism describing the unsettling sensation that time seems to accelerate as we grow older. The album focuses on the paradox behind that sensation. As Najafi explains in the accompanying interview, the music emerged from a period in which he felt psychologically frozen while time rushed relentlessly onwards. This tension between stillness and acceleration defines the album’s two long-form electroacoustic compositions. Built from live improvisations using a piezo microphone attached to an external hard drive alongside the sonification of raw digital data, Zenosyne makes surprisingly little ceremony of its unusual sound sources. The hard drive becomes another resonant object, its vibrations feeding a semi-generative system that Najafi actively steers. Algorithmic processes introduce an element of instability, but his intervention remains central to the shape of the music. The opening “Binary Bloom” begins with almost imperceptible movement. Sustained electronic tones slowly develop interference patterns and harmonic beating, gathering momentum from within. Energy and apparent speed continue to increase without reaching a conventional climax, and the accumulated tension eventually dissipates. “Static Rotation” expands this language through a more active dialogue between pure tone and electronic noise. Its materials circulate around an unstable centre, creating perpetual motion with little sense of arrival. Najafi places considerable trust in microscopic change. Much of the musical activity remains concentrated in the lower and middle registers. Rhythm and dramatic contrast play relatively small roles, while subtle redistributions of spectral energy, minute shifts in timbre and constantly evolving resonances determine the form. Musical time is stretched sufficiently for these small changes to acquire unusual weight, sharpening our awareness of its passing. To get an idea of Arshan Najafi’s live process, here is a recording of one of his no-input mixer and computer sets, followed by an interview about the making of Zenosyne. Zenosyne takes its title from John Koenig’s neologism and yet the album doesn’t seem to represent memory nostalgically. Instead, both “Binary Bloom” and “Static Rotation” seem to suspend chronological time altogether, creating spaces in which microscopic changes become more significant than linear progression. How did the idea of Zenosyne shape your compositional thinking? Were you interested in evoking the psychological sensation of accelerated time, or in constructing an alternative temporal experience in which conventional notions of duration begin to dissolve? I chose the title Zenosyne because it perfectly captured my state of mind during the composition process and still does. I was experiencing this overwhelming feeling of staying completely still – almost a sense of uselessness or incapability – while watching every day pass by in a flash of light. The music reflects that paradox. The suspension of linear time you noticed in these pieces wasn’t necessarily a conceptual design to challenge musical duration, but rather a direct mirror of that personal, psychological standstill. It is the feeling of being frozen in place while time accelerates around you. Your previous releases, from Imaginary Crisis to Live at Daa Theater House, have consistently explored live electronics, improvisation and the instability of sound in performance. Zenosyne continues that trajectory, drawing on live recordings made with a piezo microphone placed on an external hard drive alongside the sonification of raw digital data. What attracted you to treating a storage device not simply as a technological object but as a resonant instrument? Did working with the physical vibrations of digital memory alter the way you think about the relationship between information, sound and materiality? I have to admit, the reason is a bit less poetic than treating the drive as a metaphor for digital memory! I have a habit of attaching piezo mics to anything that I basically can. Frankly, I don’t see much point in recording traditional acoustic instruments anymore. That’s one of the main points of electronic music for me: it obliterates the need for conventional instruments. It gives us the freedom to choose the most mundane surface or object as a sound source and manipulate it into an entirely new form. The hard drive was just a fascinating object to harvest raw frequencies from, which the computer then allows me to further process. Both pieces were improvised live in Max/MSP before being shaped during the mixing process in Ableton Live. Listening to the album, there is a constant negotiation between systems that appear algorithmic and gestures that feel spontaneous or instinctive. How do you understand improvisation when working with generative processes? Do you see yourself directing the system, collaborating with it, or responding to behaviours that emerge unexpectedly during performance? I definitely see myself as the director of the system. I design a semi-generative algorithmic environment that responds to incoming signals based on parameters I’ve dictated beforehand. I call it “semi-generative” because I intentionally build it to a point where it still requires my interaction to continue its work; it cannot sustain itself without being steered and not sound boring to me. I view live improvisation fundamentally as a technique of composing on the fly. Because there are physical, unpredictable elements – like the random fluctuations of the hard disk spinning in “Static Rotation” – I have to remain hyper-aware and react to sudden gestures, not to mention I often cause those sudden gestures myself because I feel it’s needed at that particular moment. It’s a constant dialogue between the rules I set and the behavior the system throws back at me. Your work moves fluidly between sound, image and text—you are not only a composer but also the author of Twenty Wrong Turns. Across these different media there seems to be a recurring interest in fragmentation, ambiguity and the ways meaning emerges from incomplete information. Does Zenosyne belong to that same broader artistic inquiry? More generally, how do writing and sound composition inform one another in your practice, and are there ideas that can only be explored through one medium rather than the other? To be completely honest, I haven’t consciously intertwined my music and my writing so far. I tend to treat them as separate practices that serve different purposes. However, the connection that I do see between these mediums is the word “composition” itself, as I fundamentally treat them the same way. That’s the whole point for me. While they usually exist on their own, I might occasionally bring them together – it really just depends on how I feel about a certain project. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: When the final sound fades, the small white emblem at the bottom of the cover comes to mind. A wave reduced to calligraphy, discreet while the blue occupies everything. Wind Paths works in much the same way: it passes through the listener, leaves behind a faint vibration and entrusts the air with carrying it away. A form capable of appearing and dissolving within a few minutes Wind Paths by Philippe Deschamps   The cover already offers a statement of intent. A shifting blue, crossed by pale brushstrokes, occupies the entire field, leaving a small white mark near the lower edge. It could be water observed at close range, air made visible, a photograph taken in motion during a crossing. The image refuses to settle. Wind Paths follows the same impulse, entrusting its identity to whatever passes, bends and changes density. Philippe Deschamps gathers wind, waves and rain into music that is brief and lucid, animated by a calm that retains its sense of movement. Four pieces and just over ten minutes form a single current. The compact running time keeps every element clear of decorative contemplation. The chords move slowly, changing color by small degrees; the guitar disperses its outlines; the synthesizers hold open an even light, gently varied from within. The field recordings enter the wider fabric discreetly. Sea and rain shed their role as illustrative background and become pressure, an irregular pulse, a measure beyond human intention. The record listens to the landscape as it transforms it. The new gesture lies in the voice. Deschamps trained as a Baroque countertenor and draws on that experience here, freeing it from text. The vocal tones stretch, overlap and take on the quality of warm currents. No phrase reaches for​ meaning. The body emerges through breath, then merges with guitar and recorded air. This fusion forms the emotional centre of the EP. It offers a fragile presence. The listener recognises a human figure and immediately watches it dissolve into the broader movement. It is a simple decision on paper, decisive in its effect. Deschamps’ path has been leading towards this synthesis for some time. Introduced to the piano as a child, later a singer, bassist and guitarist in rock and post rock groups, then trained in film sound at La Fémis, the French composer has developed an ambient body of work since 2022, nourished by natural phenomena and mental images. “Blue Baths,” “Forest of my Nights,” “The Silence of Pallas,” “Remember the Clouds,” “Endless Vanishing Lines,” and “Entering the Ocean” mark the stages of a coherent inquiry. Ocean, sky, darkness and distance provide a different organizing principle each time. Wind Paths distils that inquiry even further. The voice enters the frame and alters the relationship between landscape and memory. Intensity develops through accumulation and minute alteration :: His experience in cinema emerges through the precision of each entrance and fade. Deschamps understands the weight of a sound placed an instant earlier or later, and knows how to let a detail acquire prominence without demanding it. Here, that sensitivity produces a fluid montage. Forms follow one another through affinity, carried by a slow pulse that resembles breathing and, at times, the movement of the tide. There are no spectacular peaks, refrains or turns designed to reclaim the listener’s attention. Intensity develops through accumulation and minute alteration. At certain points, a low line supports the entire field; elsewhere, the texture grows lighter and the voice seems to arrive from an immeasurable distance. Few materials, carefully chosen. The record’s ambient purity grows from this economy. Its sound world possesses body and depth, and maintains an almost tactile transparency. Silence appears within the gaps and along the fading edges of notes. Even the fuller passages leave an open area where the wind around the listener, distant traffic or movement elsewhere in the house can still be heard. The music welcomes such intrusions. Its open character encourages a porous relationship with the present. Wind Paths can drift at low volume and preserve its identity; under closer listening, it reveals subtle changes, harmonies slipping sideways and voices layered with restraint. Such control brings its own risk. At times, the music’s gentleness brushes against a beauty held too safely, polished until friction and surprise have almost disappeared. Its brevity sharpens the issue: certain openings withdraw just as they acquire an unexpected inflection. The ending arrives early and leaves a desire for one further stretch, perhaps a little less serene. This limitation also clarifies the nature of the project. Wind Paths chooses a form capable of appearing and dissolving within a few minutes. It asks for attention without insisting upon it. The title speaks of invisible paths, and the music realizes that idea with remarkable coherence. Each element follows its own direction, guided by shared currents. The voice rises, the guitar fades, the harmonies change their angle. Deschamps has created one of his most lucid works, bringing together his vocal training, cinematic sensibility and ambient practice within a form that feels accessible, intimate and precise. When the final sound fades, the small white emblem at the bottom of the cover comes to mind. A wave reduced to calligraphy, discreet while the blue occupies everything. Wind Paths works in much the same way: it passes through the listener, leaves behind a faint vibration and entrusts the air with carrying it away. Wind Paths is available on Silent Sonic. [Bandcamp] Wind Paths by Philippe DeschampsThe post Philippe Deschamps :: Wind Paths (Silent Sonic) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Hawgood has tied Folk Reels to the idea of a mobile archive, a repository for scattered works, old tapes and encounters. Live At Still Point 2026 introduces a welcome fissure into that archive. To preserve also means admitting loss and giving it an audible measure. A work that fully embraces the loss it suffered and transforms it into living matter Live at Still Point 2026 by Ian Hawgood   A live album promises to bear witness, a weighty claim, perhaps too weighty. It evokes the idea of an event fixed once and for all, destined to return unchanged with every listen. Live At Still Point 2026 favors a memory with sections erased, passages heard only by those present at Brimscombe Mill that afternoon. The recording preserves the core of Ian Hawgood’s performance, while the contributions of two laptops used for processing were never captured in the file. A tangible absence, then, which has become the defining character of the work itself. The released sound recognizes its own limits and reveals them with rare candor. For Hawgood, the concert marked his return to performing before an audience after seven years. That fact carries more weight than a line in a press release, since his artistic journey has always sought a human dimension in the act of listening. A British sound engineer, founder of Home Normal and custodian of Folk Reels, he has built an extensive catalog around care, collaboration, tape and field recordings. At Still Point, that principle reconnects with the risk of the moment and a freedom still capable of play. Twenty five minutes, a single movement. At first come rustling sounds, calls whose source is difficult to place, brief electrical flashes. They​ resemble tentative contacts taking the measure of the air. Then a deep mass expands, gathering everything happening around it. Figures from We Are But Dream are bent and pushed towards a different sense of duration. Hawgood uses SYNTRX, Buchla sequences, sounds gathered outdoors and computers running AudioMulch, instruments from different eras surrendering their names to a single current. The music grows unhurriedly and gathers body through accumulation. A melody seems about to declare itself, then immediately chooses a less determinate form. This hesitation gives the work its intensity. No backdrop inviting distraction, no contemplative postcard. Hawgood’s ambient music asks for attention in a low voice and makes perceptible the time sound requires to change its nature. From time to time, an impulse punctures the continuity, an oblique jolt roughens the balance. It happens, that is all. The performance retains a vulnerable quality, even a slight awkwardness, precious in an age obsessed with polish. Depth becomes almost physical :: In the central stretch, depth becomes almost physical. The volume rises, the fabric thickens, while the pressure avoids all monumental emphasis. Hawgood proceeds through successive degrees of proximity: one colour enters another, the drone slowly alters its light, the breathing becomes irregular. It takes time to realize that the initial landscape is already elsewhere. At the point of greatest rarefaction, the current loses substance and seems about to fade out. The music accepts this descent. From there emerge more clearly defined figures, a gentle pulse, circling scales that bring energy without breaking the spell. The ending gathers motion and a strange, purposeful serenity, as though the sound had found a way to continue after almost dispersing. Tim Diagram’s photograph translates this condition well. Trees seen from below, pale clouds, a second pattern of foliage superimposed upon the sky. The image holds two temporalities and allows them to interfere. The album likewise contains what happens and the imprint of what escapes. The material lost from the two computers compels a reconsideration of what a document can mean. The audience heard a broader version, traversed by elements that are now irretrievable; the album offers an autonomous trajectory, barer and perhaps more exposed. Fidelity lies in the gesture, its openness to chance and the human scale of what has been preserved. Hawgood has tied Folk Reels to the idea of a mobile archive, a repository for scattered works, old tapes and encounters. Live At Still Point 2026 introduces a welcome fissure into that archive. To preserve also means admitting loss and giving it an audible measure. The still point evoked by the title becomes a magnetic centre around which everything changes: intensity, distance, density, memory. This is where the album’s achievement lies. Its beauty arises from a restrained decision: to release what survived without consoling reconstruction and to entrust absence with an active role. At the end, an unusual feeling lingers. Has one listened to a concert, or to the memory that a concert produced inside a machine? The question matters more than any answer. Hawgood offers twenty five minutes freed from the pose of the celebratory live album and the smoothness of the ambient product. The sound breathes, falters, gathers strength and recedes. In that movement it carries with it the Still Point community, the apprehension of returning, the pleasure of experimentation and the part that no medium will ever be able to hold. A work that fully embraces the loss it suffered and transforms it into living matter. Live at Still Point 2026 is available on folk reels. items.body: Giulio Aldinucci has made an album that seems acquainted with the unnamed part of human nature, the part that surfaces in sleep or in the few seconds before news capable of changing the course of a day. Rhythm is felt through changes in pressure Materia by GIULIO ALDINUCCI   At first there is weight. A quiet, almost geological pressure that arrives before recognition, touching the body before it reaches the mind. Materia begins in that dark place. Sound has volume, temperature, even something resembling a will of its own. It advances slowly and alters the scale of things, like a sudden bank of fog moving in. Sight loses its authority and the ear becomes a larger organ. Giulio Aldinucci has made an album that seems acquainted with the unnamed part of human nature, the part that surfaces in sleep or in the few seconds before news capable of changing the course of a day. The composer, born in Siena, Tuscany, reaches this point after years devoted to landscape, memory and the voice stripped of semantic meaning. The experience developed under the name Obsil and the chapter that began with Tarsia have shaped a coherent body of work, nourished by field recordings, choral presences and electronic transformations. Borders And Ruins examined the nature of territory; Disappearing In A Mirror and Shards Of Distant Times shifted the tension towards identity and memory; Real sought a personal reality within the excess of digital mediation. Materia, Aldinucci’s fifth album for Karlrecords, condenses that history into an essential gesture: taking a tightly packed mass of sound, carving into it, paring it back and searching for what is already alive​ inside. The album was released on September 18, 2026. Here accumulation and subtraction become emotional acts. Aldinucci gathers frequencies as scattered memories might be gathered after years apart, then removes the excess and listens into the space left behind by what has disappeared. Time, too, acquires substance. It is broken into minute units and reassembled according to an order that escapes the familiar pulse. Rhythm is felt through changes in pressure, through inner tides, through the way a distant voice rises from the haze and immediately loses its face. These are slow movements filled with secret life. Their apparent stillness is alive with motion. The six pieces form a single body lasting just under 43 minutes. Density remains the active principle, capable of changing state while retaining its gravity. The depths below sustain the journey with a telluric continuity. Above them appear distorted choirs, echoes, drifting particles and sounds that preserve a human trace after language and origin have fallen away. The titles sketch a constellation of absence: “Not Here,” the shadow cast by noise, ash and distant waves, the absolute finality of “Never,” evening, then light caught in a dream. The music receives these images and preserves their indeterminacy. Each one works within the act of listening, removed from plot and close to the freedom of involuntary association. “Materia finds its human center here. The album’s grandeur springs from this dizzying proportion: an immense sound holds a tiny gesture, perhaps a mouth drawing breath, perhaps a syllable worn away by time.” ~Mirco Salvadori The voice is central. It rises like a collective memory without face or biography, suspended between comfort and alarm. At times it resembles someone calling across an immense distance; elsewhere it takes on the substance of a thought formed in the body before words. Aldinucci understands the power of vocal fragments and frees them from any narrative duty. What remains is breath, impulse, a tremor that reminds the listener of human fragility. Materia finds its human center here. The album’s grandeur springs from this dizzying proportion: an immense sound holds a tiny gesture, perhaps a mouth drawing breath, perhaps a syllable worn away by time. “Come Luce, In Sogno,” chosen as the advance single, offers a discreet way into the album. The light invoked by its title contains dust and density. It filters through opaque layers and produces figures already moving towards dissolution. Dreaming becomes a mode of knowledge. A detail can expand until it fills the entire field of perception, while an enormous event contracts into a brief vibration. This instability runs through the whole work. Time seems to lengthen; then an almost imperceptible shift alters the landscape. Sound retains warmth and a question that has yet to find words. The cover helps reveal the character of the work. A white façade multiplies concave modules, dark openings and curves that look identical only at a glance. The eye finds order, then differences, shadows, stains and minor signs of wear. It is a serial form made vulnerable by time and by the material from which it is built. Aldinucci’s music behaves in much the same way. It turns repetition into change, raises immense structures and allows irregularity to bring them alive. Each surface hints at another depth. No answer comes. The desire to look again grows stronger. The concentration of the sound demands complete attention. A moment’s distraction can break the spell, and some passages deliberately court saturation. This is an exacting choice. Materia requires time, an appropriate volume and a measure of solitude. In return it offers a rare experience, moving listening beyond taste and into consciousness. Its forms entrust their appeal to a slower force, like the memory of a place never visited. There is familiarity and a faint fear. The unknown takes on an intimate temperature. “Sound appears as something that precedes its maker and continues beyond its listener, bound to the same matter as bodies, air and thought.” ~Mirco Salvadori Throughout Aldinucci’s career, recording the world has carried the value of a living archive. A landscape could hold a story; a procession could deliver into the present voices already receding into the distance; an ordinary noise could open a passage through perception. Materia brings this practice close to an elemental dimension. Here substance comes before place and contact before narrative. Sound appears as something that precedes its maker and continues beyond its listener, bound to the same matter as bodies, air and thought. This is where its power lies. The album speaks of the human condition through feeling. The need to give chaos a shape meets the fascination of whatever resists a final form. Every cut removes part of the original mass; subtraction reveals an unforeseen outline. The music breathes between these impulses, tightens, withdraws and fills out again. At times it seems about to disclose something. Then that something changes substance and becomes pure listening. Materia is expansive, gathered into a fierce intensity and charged with physical mystery. Giulio Aldinucci reaches one of the most mature expressions of his artistic language and gives contemporary ambient music an album with moral as well as sonic weight. When the final vibration ends, silence feels altered, thicker, almost conscious. Within that silence passes an intuition that cannot quite be held: perhaps the human spirit is precisely this restless substance, seeking form while knowing that every form is temporary. For just under 43 minutes, Materia gives it a body and lets it sing. Materia is available on Karlrecords. items.body: Kim Cascone’s book Post-Digital Music gives sound artists the conceptual thought tools that help open up connective valves between the unconscious and conscious minds, stimulating the growth of imagination. This collection of essays is also essential reading for the continued critical discourse around issues of electronic music production and reception. Beyond knobs, plugins, and technique Some books about music making take a very materialist approach. They look at sound as a purely physical phenomenon. They look at art making as just a matter of sliding the right dials and turning the right knobs (and they love to turn knobs). They ignore the subtle side of being a musician, the synchronistic clues that align to tell an artist they are on the right path of creation, the inner knowing of when to start on a certain project, when to halt on another one, and when it might be good to revive a work left behind. There are enough books that focus on the hardware and software of music making, even as they ignore the realware of imagination. Without imagination such tools mean little or nothing. Kim Cascone’s book Post-Digital Music gives sound artists the conceptual thought tools that help open up connective valves between the unconscious and conscious minds, stimulating the growth of imagination. This collection of essays is also essential reading for the continued critical discourse around issues of electronic music production and reception. Electronic music isn’t about having a stylish se​t of tools, a modular set up that looks good on social media, or a digital studio with all the latest plugins. The tools won’t accomplish much without a musician who has grown what Goethe called “new organs of perception.” This is a phrase Cascone uses throughout his writing as a way to convey the necessity of training intuitive skills, skills at noticing the subtle, skills that can help an individual create pieces resonate with the interior life of their prospective audience, rather than just regurgitate shiny audio baubles whose sounds never reach beneath the surface.None of this is to discount the training and skill set needed to develop as a musician, songwriter or composer on the material level, but it has been shown again and again that people without the traditional pedigree of talent and virtuosity can make compelling music, while the works of virtuoso’s can be lifeless and boring. Technical chops are only half the battle. If it was all about technique, Hollywood movies would be a lot better than they are and so-called B-Films from the past would suck, but I’ve found the opposite to be true. A mind and spirit keyed in to the imaginative side of the world allows an artist in any medium to tune their own subtle senses to act as antennae for incoming seeds and ideas. Once transmuted those seeds can then be recast into the field of cultural life. The eighteen essays collected in Post-Digital Music act as a corrective to the material focus prevalent in so much of electronic music discourse over the past several decades. The essays themselves span the years 1999 to 2026 and show the evolution of Cascone’s mature thought. Many of these pieces have been around in various publications and posted online, and I had read a good chunk of them over the years before this slim volume arrived. It’s nice to have them collected all in one place, and the book can easily be tucked into a laptop bag or backpack to peruse between setting up for different gigs, recording sessions or any other time when an injection of deep thought or intellectual stimulation is required. Issues that Cascone brings up in the first short essay, “Residualism,” crop up throughout the work and are looked at from different angles all the way to the last essay “0’00” and Vertical Time.” And while they are organized sequentially in the order they were written, I have found that there are about three main topics, along with various interrelated subfields, that the essays flock and organize themselves around. The first of these topics, and a major overarching theme of his work in general is one many people are afraid to look at: failure. Cascone looks at “The Aesthetics of Failure,” ruminates on “Modulating the Boundaries of Failure” and pokes around into the possibility of failure as a window from which the future leaks out in “Errormancy: Glitch as Divination.” After a few decades of thinking about failure, and working with it in artistic computer music, he still hadn’t extracted or unpacked all that could be gleaned from its study. He included an interview titled “The Failure of Failure,” which goes beyond the notion of working with software at the edges of their prescribed ability, and takes a critical look at the failure of experimental music and art to glitch out the larger system of society. Perhaps the failure of these genres and subgenres within electronic music to change things in larger society also relates to the continued problems around performing electronic music. His essay “Laptop Music” traces the issues around live electronic music performance, specifically with computers, and it remains just as pertinent as it was when it was written in 2004. He quickly delineates the history of different kinds of music performance in the west, showing how the placing of electronic musicians on stages, and the audience in seats, as in your typical theater situation, upsets our notions of what a music performance is and should be. By way of example, I had the opportunity to see William Basinski earlier this year, and he played in a theater. He was on the stage with a tape loop, a laptop and a mixing board. I was very happy to hear this music done live, and I sat with my eyes closed for most of the show as the sounds washed over me at volumes levels I would never breach at home. When I didn’t have my eyes closed, I mostly paid attention to his video projections. His adjustments of the mixing board, computer, and loop were all very understated, and the video was in many respects its own kind of visual drone. Yet even as a fan of him, and even as someone who has played electronic music live myself with laptops and other knobby gear, the expectation around of musical performance as a kind of visual spectacle of virtuosity remain in place. As Cascone put it, “The laptop musician is conceived as a medium conducting a séance, whose tricks of table knocks, wall rapping and spectral voices broadcast from nowhere are orchestrated to feign the effect of authenticity where none really exists. Thus the cultural artifact produced by the laptop musician is deemed a counterfeit, leaving the audience unable to determine a use-value.” There still has not been much a “recuperation of codes that move away from the use of spectacle, that establish aura, and show the audience how to differentiate ‘representation by the machine’ from ‘repetition of the machine.’” Many in the audience relied on the aura of expectation created by Basinski’s albums in the live setting, or on his comedic pre and post show banter as a way to come away from the evening feeling satisfied. “The laptop musician is conceived as a medium conducting a séance, whose tricks of table knocks, wall rapping and spectral voices broadcast from nowhere are orchestrated to feign the effect of authenticity where none really exists. Thus the cultural artifact produced by the laptop musician is deemed a counterfeit, leaving the audience unable to determine a use-value.” ~Kim Cascone The other early essays remain just as relevant. The issues Cascone raised, now decades ago, are still with us. Sometimes there has been a bit of mutation along the fringes of the field, but where things have remained static, the major points are still at play. It must be remembered that electronic music is still very young as an art. The post-digital is even younger with its general focus on computer music. Perhaps a definition of just what Cascone means by Post-Digital is in order. In “Residualism” he talks about how Post-Digital music making is about the “deconstruction of audio by manipulating the prima materia itself” and how this has led to the recognition of the aesthetic value of sonic artifacts that were previously considered to be in the background. The art becomes a matter of subtracting information until only residues are left behind. While this simplifies the theoretical basis Cascone lays out, this approach and its aesthetic ramifications can be considered another core theme of the book. Because those artifacts had often been generated by pushing technology and software to the breaking point, is one of the reasons behind his intense focus failure, and how it can be a gateway into new forms of aesthetics. Another theme that emerges is a trinity around music, metaphysics and imagination. There is spiritual substance in the book, and in the works created by artists who are tuned in to the subtle fields. Essays in this grouping of include “Subtle Listening,” a text based on the workshops Cascone used to give. (These differ in form and substance from Pauline Oliveros’ work with Deep Listening, though I see the two as complimentary.) He also explores the metaphysical side in pieces such as “The Avantgarde as Aeromancy” and “The Transcenditial Imagination.” Other pieces such as “Organs of Subtle Perception” and “Imagination, Idea, Will, Manifestation” get to some of the core precepts around his percepts. His essay on aeromancy written in 2013 reflects on the artists relationship to time. Over on the blog at the Silent Records Bandcamp page, Cascone continues to write about time, about the hyper-present and how the effects of the simulacra and our immersion in online worlds pushes us into a vertical experience of time. He distinguishes this sense of verticality, of being removed from the clock-a-day world of linear horizontal time, from the kind of natural verticality we experience in moments of creative flow and time spent outside in nature.For the artist working on the horizons, at the boundaries, these distinctions are important for the work of tuning into the subtle senses and fishing for big ideas. In the essay he writes, “The past has become embedded in the future, reducing what we experience as ‘the present’ or ‘now’ -as simulacra, a plastic bauble bouncing upon the infinitesimal fulcrum where two streams intersect. One beckons from the past, the other seduces from the future. The plastic bauble of ‘now’ is all that exists today. All of time is trapped inside of it, containing a chimeric environment constructed from a trick of light, a sleight of hand, a conflation of nostalgic past with a tantalizing future.” And he continues with this salient advice: “For a real avant-garde to exist -again- we need to reestablish a ‘long-view’ perspective, recover from our collective amnesia, and locate ourselves in the larger historical landscape. By moving outside the manufactured environment and allowing the stream of time full passage through our psyches, we can return to an intuitive process of artistic divination.” “Like the artist, the audience also needs to be able to open the valve to the unconscious. Digital media in its current incarnation works as a firehose blasting the senses. Overstimulation is part of the issue. To tune in, sometimes the first step isn’t turning on, but turning off.” ~Justin Patrick Moore Now we are even more in the blurspace of the simulacra than we were in 2013. For those of us who wish to see such a return of the avant-garde as Cascone does we need to take regular time for reflection. If one of the tasks of the artist is to give reflection back, gestation periods are necessary, as is frequent time spent outside the outer focused hyper-present world, and inside the inner focused world of imagination. What bubbles inside the cauldron of a new avant-garde may take time to brew. In the world of outer of immediate action where each new piece and release vies for attention with the rest, the long term view tends to get shunted off and replaced by short term commodification, i.e. the market forces that cultivate the hyper-present simulacra for their own harvest. The larger gains that come from time spent swimming in the reflecting pool of imagination are not as apparent, not as immediate, but the long term effects could be much larger than those produced by the shiny baubles of momentary attention. For every force there is a field, and for the final grouping of general ideas I see in this book is the cluster around these words: aura, grain, and field. Field recordings have been at the heart of many approaches to electronic music for quite some time starting with the academic part of the tradition. Following the explosion of electronica, ambient, and then the plethora of interconnected subgenres, many electronicists began employing field recordings as a way to lend their pieces an organic integrity they sometimes lacked when based purely on digital sources. Ideas around the use of field recordings, and what a field actually is, all get explored at a deep theoretical level that is often missing elsewhere in the discourse. Along the way we get to learn about Cybernetics and Systems Theory (always fun and always essential) as well as flocks and the swarming behavior of genres, and how they form. All of these subjects tend to get woven into each other, one area emphasized here, another there. Reading them together, it is hard not to feel the desire to get creative. The intellectual stimulation gives me the desire to put more critical imagination into the work of making electronic music and the conversations around the field. Perhaps the greatest advice to the aspiring artist included in the book is to “lessen ones dependence on digital tools” and his admonition, via Werner Herzog, to “Read, read, read…” he suggests that composers be “voracious readers and keep a physical notebook of ideas and projects. By relying less on digital tools you will gain a valuable context for your work.” That in itself is very much another kind of Post-Digital framework. As the book began with focusing perceptions on the boundaries and edges in “Residualism,, so it ends with a piece focusing on one of the great Zen koans John Cage left behind in the form of a musical composition. It is a seldom talked about piece of music that he wrote, 0”00”. It is a work that has no duration, and in many ways, it only exists in the mind. By going back to this ground zero, we are left in a kind of recursive mobius strip, zeroing back in on zero itself. Cascone again cautions against getting too caught up in the speed race of digital acceleration. He also reminds us that the collective suite of digital tools that now exist to make things by command, i.e., AI, while in some ways resembling the chance operations and recombinatorial procedures of the earlier avant-garde expemplified by John Cage, do not in fact resemble the actual facts of his work. Cage did his chance operations in a slowed down way. His use of the I Ching was part of a contemplative artistic process, not just punching in commands at a whim. As such, until we can regain our composure and pull ourselves away from the immersive grip of the hyperattentive state induced by the constant influx of media and data made possible by what Cascone has often called McGovCorp, it will remain difficult for sophisticated artworks in any medium to find a receptive audience. Like the artist, the audience also needs to be able to open the valve to the unconscious. Digital media in its current incarnation works as a firehose blasting the senses. Overstimulation is part of the issue. To tune in, sometimes the first step isn’t turning on, but turning off. Post-Digital Music (Essays) is available on Silent Records. [Bandcamp]The post Kim Cascone :: Post-Digital Music: Essays (1999–2026) (Silent) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: To complement her interview in The Wire 512, Slovenian improvising pianist and bandleader Kaja Draksler creates an exclusive Wire mix Kaja Draksler studied jazz at a music-oriented high school in Ljubljana, later enrolling at the Conservatory of Amsterdam. There, her instructor, the British composer Richard Ayres, asked her the simple question,“What do you want to do?”, which set her on a path that would chafe against the jazz orthodoxy. In August Punkt.Vrt. Plastik, her long-running trio with Swedish bassist Petter Eldh and German drummer Christian Lillinger, released their fourth album, Kompress, while another of her groups, matter 100, releases its debut True Or False this October. This exclusive mix, she explains, is “more of a collage, where I mostly take excerpts from different pieces, placing them one after the other, and, at times, one of top of the other. The track selection is a mix of my own music and music I love, with a bit of a focus on piano and voices.” Tracklist Kaja Draksler “Prst, roka, laket” (excerpt) Vaqif Mustafazadə “Bizim Bakı Gecələri” (excerpt) Luciano Berio “A La Femminisca” Christian Lillinger “Poliform” (excerpt) Punkt.Vrt.Plastik “EKV” Vince Staples “Get Paid” New London Chamber Choir & James Wood “Serment” (excerpt) Georges Aperghis “Recitation 10_ left part, 1st version” Nina Simone “Who Am I” Irena Z Tomažin “Rain” (excerpt) Pauline Oliveros “Horse Sings From A Cloud” (excerpt) J Gallus “Mirabile Misterium: De Nativitate Circumcisione Et Epiphania Domini Huelgas Ensemble” matter 100 “Rushing Through The Night” (excerpt) Czajka & Puchacz “Wacky Compass” (excerpt(s)) MIA “Sunshowers” (excerpt) Cecil Taylor “Pt 4 Glossalalia” (excerpt) Craig Taborn “Glossolalia” Kaja Draksler Octet “Come See” (excerpt) Andrew Parrot “De Torrente” Judith Berkson “Castle” Ellen Arkbro “For Organ And Brass” (excerpt) matter 100 “Alternating Current” Read Peter Margasak’s full interview with Kaja Draksler in The Wire 512. Pick up a copy in our online shop. Subscribers can read the full article in the digital archive here.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — An unusual yet fully-progressive undertaking of setting literary stories to music using jazz-fusion artists.1. "The Sinking Spell" (4:40) Robert Wyatt's distinctive voice enters with some effect applied while the four musicians, Steve Swallow, Jack DeJohnette, Carla Bley, and Terje Rypdal apply their talents to constructing a loose and reactive soundtrack to Robert's rendering of this Edward Gorey story. Terje is particularly flamboyant (almost in a Steve Hackett way!) while Carla, Steve, and Jack are pretty dynamic in their own right. Perhaps Robert's best, most unique performance on the album and maybe the best collective Jazz-Rock Fusionary exposition as well. (9.125/10) 2. "The Object Lesson" (5:00) piano, bass and swelling cymbal crashes back Robert's rather flat/monotone delivery of this story. Eventually the musicians fall into a kind of groove with Jack DeJohnette's rock drumming and Terje Rypdal and Carla Bley's Canterbury organ saw-like expressions. The music is not great, not fully-formed or composed for much other than dramatic support, but it works (it's better than the story being told). (8.75/10)3 "The Insect God" (5:00) some truly top-notch Jazz-Rock Fusion is used to present another sobering and not-for-children's-ears story. The music quartet of Bley, Rypdal, Swallow, and drummer Jack DeJohnette are all on the same page of aggressive and insistent delivery while Robert and spoken-word "backing vocalists" render their fast-talking approach to dramatic story-telling. (8.75/10)4 "The Doubful Guest" (4:45) finally! some thoroughly-composed music! It's a challenging weave of off-timed hi-speed drum and keyboard music in which Steve and Terje contribute long-held, pensive notes on their respective instruments. All the while Robert delivers a near-spoken word story with a little more flair and enthusiasm than the past two. The overall weave really works--has no glaring flaws or inconsistencies. I like the way the musical performances ramp up toward the end: especially Terje's guitar shredding and Carla's breadth of synth strings chords. (9.125/10)5 "The Remembered Visit" (6:25) voice with syncopated bass and synth-strings pulses, adding piano and Mellotron "ooo"s and "aaah"s, then treated electric guitar notes and some background drumming. In the third minute the drums and bass play get more animated--still orchestral and reactive, though, more than "song" oriented. Where Robert's delivery starts out dramatic and engaged, it begins to sound a bit like rote reading in places. But then things slow down for the background vocal-supported passage in the fifth minute--which has the effect of seeming to bring Robert back into the spirit of the story. From there out he feels fully-present in his story-telling. Effective. (8.875/10)6 "The Hapless Child" (7:00) Robert Wyatt's distinctive voice and vocal/story-telling stylings are here backed by music that feels more like theater music: it's incidental and yet has a personality all its own--as if taking on the characteristics of Robert's story's characters. Nothing is flowing or timed, almost all of it feels impressionistic and reactive more than composed and prescribed. There is one theme that feels prepared: the whole-band motif that starts at 2:58 when Robert starts singing about the start of Charlotte Sophia's boarding school experience, but at 4:20 everything devolves to simple piano--just before launching into a more dynamic and drum-and-guitar-driven theme. What a horrifying Dickensian tale! Carla Bley's odd chord choices hold the whole thing down but it's Steve Swallow's obtuse bass notes and Terje Rypdal's sharp, stinging guitar notes that bring forth and amplify the Poe-like atmosphere of the story. Wow! What an experience! Definitely not your typical bed-time story! Even children's theatre would be scarred and marred for decades if they brought children in to hear this one! Still, it is a rather powerful and effective delivery mechanism. (13.25/15)Total Time:I have to admit that I was not prepared for either the album's total dedication to story telling nor it's dark and rather dismal, even desolate, Dickensian/Brothers Grimm/Edgar Allen Poe story lines. While I love the literate nature of the stories, I'm a bit disturbed by their unsettling subject matters. At the same time, I appreciate these adventurous musicians for their commitment to the expansion of that which music and Jazz-Rock Fusion can do. B/four stars; though admirable to take on such an odd and ambitious undertaking, I feel that the stories and music do not always match as well as the artists/producers may have wanted. Nor are the instrumental performances and song/soundtrack compositions as polished and coordinated as well as one might expect or desire from this stellar line-up.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A surprisingly-sophisticated and highly-entertaining album from a group of University of Illinois college students! Released on Brunswick Records in July of 1972.1. "The Monster Bride" (10:36) a very proggy, early King Crimson and Yes-like opening of bass, organ, clarinet, and delicate cymbal play turns in the second minute toward proggy brass rock--more like ELP meets BS&T. In the third minute the motif starts to smooth out before suddenly switching direction toward more light and playful circus music and then, in the fourth minute there is an equally sudden directional change toward more avant/eclectic Jazz-Rock Fusion before going Crimson and Zappa in the fifth. This is all quite tightly-performed and very sophisticated and unpredictable! It must have been something to compose and then pull off as a band in 1970s studio conditions. By the time we get to the end of the sixth minute everything slows down to a cymbal-supported droning organ for a Peter Hammill-like male vocal to enter and sing. Very Crimsonian! Flute and piano pick up from here with a very pretty, almost CHICAGO-like melody presentation and passage which builds and builds, horns entering and gathering forces over bass, guitar, and drum's rhythm track. At 5:22 everything stops for some percussion-backed dramatic very theatric narration of a sexually-piqued scene of the monster's reaction and response to the birth of his bride and child--which then leads to a finishing burst of CHICAGO-like brass rock. Very interesting! The sophistication of the compositions (and ability to pull it off in the studio) is the most impressive part. (18.375/20) 2. "Spiders (In Neals Basement)" (5:57) an accented male voice singing a sly lyric of film noir's detective-type music, like musical themes for scenes in a New Orleans juke joint or Chicago flop house. The music, performances both instrumentally and vocally are so colorful and spry. Great brassy theater music and great entertainment! Amazing that these were just a bunch of college kids! (9.333/10)3. "Witches Theme And Dance" (9:47) a brass rock song that opens like a LIGHTHOUSE song with great pace and energy before dropping down into a slow, plodding motif over which the gang issue some great four-part vocal harmony vocals. These guys must've done music theater or high school theater music. Bassist Neal Rosner is quite impressive (and, thankfully, placed forward in the mix), sounding a lot like Goblin or PFM's bassists. More stunning theatric stop-and-start composition performed with ease and professional precision over/within which electric guitar, voices, slide flute, and other mildly scary Hallowe'en noises contribute their solos and incidentals. Nice trilly flute solo in the final third--augmented by awesome "distant" flugelhorn. The finish is just perfect for the "lesson" of the witchy allegory. Another gem of a song; these guys are so creative and so talented! (18.875/20)4. "A Brief Message From Your Local Media" (9:59) here the band conjures up a four-part suite. It opens sounding like something from Aaron Copeland before organ, bass, hi-hat & bass drum lay down a soft carpet for a lone vocalist to begin his GREG LAKE-like "In the Court of the Crimson King" imitation. Obligatory flute joins in as "Greg" reaches his third verse--arpeggiated guitar chords and increasingly MICHAEL GILES-like drumming, as well. Around 4:30 there is a break in which narrator delivers a brief spoken-word summation of the contributions of Henry Ford to the workings of modern society, which is then followed by the development of a new motif of rather up-tempo organ- and flute-driven Jazz-Rock--which gains Latin elements in the eighth minute to give it a LEONARD BERNSTEIN West Side Story feel but then about a minute later the music moves more toward a pop/theatric-Brass Rock form similar to the snarky Hair, Godspel, and Pippen phenomenons. The music ends with a fading out calliope and military drums sound. Interesting. Though still delightfully creative and astonishingly sophisticated, the cohesiveness of this one is questionable (but, then, so is the flow of the typical radio or television programming!). (18.125/20) - a) "The Garden"- b) "The Assembly Line"- c) "Electric Man"- d) "Question"Total time 36:19Jazzy, brassy Crimsonian prog rock that sounds quite mature for a bunch of Illini students--and it's so entertaining, even addictive! Incredible for a debut album.A/five stars; a surprisingly-sophisticated and well-polished display of delightfully-entertaining compositions and performances. Who knew?! And, Whatever happened to?

items.body: Review by alainPP — Green Carnation presents the third album in the "A Dark Poem" trilogy, nodding to the likes of Anathema and Katatonia. It delivers an oppressive, heavy, and meditative sound with dark progressive roots."Unconditional Artificial Chemistry" opens with a spacey feel, suddenly cut through by an exuberant, thick, heavy guitar; the monolithic vocals help transport the listener to another planet. The track narrates the dangers of AI, unfolding seamlessly while building an all-encompassing, progressive intensity. It shifts to include a crystalline piano in the distance, with musical grandeur that straddles the line between doom and Opeth-esque gothic metal, creating an oppressive atmosphere. There is a spellbinding melancholy'a blend of Anathema, Mogwai, Katatonia, and early King Crimson. "The Messiah Complex" features a melting guitar arpeggio, with vocals that abruptly break the ethereal, charming, and hypnotic mood. Melancholic, mysterious keyboards add a layer of solemnity that oozes progressive structure, while the dominant vocals allow the mantra-like atmosphere to spill over. The decrescendo finale is simple and effective'steady and unstoppable'serving as a musical paradigm."Broken Souls, Common Enemies" features a prominent New Wave-style synth driving the rhythm. The riff, the languid vocals, and the guitar's plaintive melody evoke emotion, discovery, and complexity in a track that is heavy without flaunting it. A shift to screamed vocals over a machine-gun riff'reminiscent of The Gathering in their early days'reasserts the track's intensity and complexity, bolstered by Wright-esque keyboards. A break featuring an ethereal flute and a melting, Western-style acoustic solo follows. Vocoded vocals amplify the majestic atmosphere, launching a stratospheric guitar solo worthy of the genre's titans'a truly stunning moment. Finally, "A Dark Poem - Orchestral Suite" begins with otherworldly vocals introducing wind instruments'including Ingrid's flute'as the orchestral arrangement takes center stage. An orchestral suite worthy of *Fantasia*'a classic pastoral anthem recounting Rimbaud's "Ophelia," performed by the Kristiansand Symphony Orchestra and its opera choir. Then comes the break: a return to archaic vocals, a primal sound reaching its zenith'is this the birth of prog? A dark, unsettling, yet colorful and pastoral atmosphere, pierced by illuminating trumpets; it is a masterpiece right up to the final note, with a soaring violin flourish creating a moment that transcends time.Green Carnation takes its final bow with this triptych finale'punchier, spellbinding, and invigorating. It is a crowning achievement, blending dystopian lyrics about our society with majestic, solemn melodies. Classy, ​​dreamlike, and immense progressive post-metal'featuring a sound that left an indelible mark on me from their very beginnings, delivering a powerful impact this September.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Despite having been around for some thirty years (their first album, released in 1993, was produced by Eroc, former drummer of Grobschnitt), very little has been written about this German band in the progressive music press, with the exception of a few wonderfully insightful reviews published in 2001 to mark the release of their masterpiece, *Fantasma*. In those insightful lines, everything was said?from the impeccable vocals of Oliver Philipps?the heart and soul of the band?which stir us with emotion in airy, nostalgic atmospheres, to Everon's distinctive taste for Rush at its most melodic. Incidentally, the influence of the fathers of Canadian hard-prog on a band from our good old continent is rare enough to warrant special mention. For good measure, among the similarities or influences more or less acknowledged by Everon, we should also mention the prog metal of Vanden Plas, the even more symphonic style of Sylvan, or the more neo-prog sound of Pallas. And despite my fear of intriguing or horrifying some readers, I'll also take the liberty of pointing out Oliver Philipps's avowed fondness (see his website) for Nik Kershaw.But it's through a subtle affinity for Rush that *North* really bursts onto the scene, with a mind-blowing and compact "Hands ", driven by an unstoppable melody yet free of any lulls or orchestral flourishes (here, a few keyboards with a discreet but essential presence)?exactly as Oliver Philipps intended, having momentarily had his fill of his own sumptuous arrangements.A track remarkable for its ability to encapsulate the very best of its creator's aspirations, "Hands" reassures us of Everon's intentions: to succeed in creating something that is both simple and grandiose. This is something the band's two previous albums, *Flesh* and *Bridge*?which were not substantial enough despite the extravagant 14-minute title track "Flesh"?partially failed to achieve; curiously, both were released in the same year (2002). The next track, "A Brief Encounter", is the biggest surprise on the new album: constructed like a sort of "Turn of the Century" in tune with our times (read: with a testosterone boost), complete with acoustic guitar and piano parts, it unabashedly reveals the depth of Philips' love for the universal sound of Yes. The greatest (and consistent) melodic shortcoming?at least on the early albums?has, over time, become a strength. Straight to the point: emotion. UnforgettableOliver is a tremendous singer who has never stopped improving since a debut album that was nearly disastrous in that regard (a young Greg Lake's voice, uncertain and poorly anchored to confusing melodies) to reach a level that only the very best have attained. On that note, on *North*, be sure to listen to "Test of Time", opulent prog metal with a brief cello intro. Or the tormented "North" ("I remember I wrote 'North' on an unbelievably stormy day" (O. Philipps), with its false string section richer than a cathedral door.Olivier Philipps is also an excellent musician (guitars, keyboards) who puts his performance at the service of the richness of the melody?and not the other way around. He's fairly sparing with solos but increasingly generous with pure emotion, as on "Wasn't It Good" (6:33), the most poignant track on *North*, my favorite track, and probably also Oliver Philipps's favorite on this album: "Actually, in my humble personal opinion, this kind of song is the essence of what Everon is all about" (O. Philipps). At the beginning, with a touch of nostalgia, a piano begins to float heavily through the ether, the melody detached from its harmonic body, a sphere of thought undulating at the end of a long string. And when the guitar solo comes in?which seems as simple as pie, so much so that even my thick, clumsy little fingers think they can play it?you find yourself hoping never to hear another lukewarm review of Everon.The edgy "Woodworks", a highly successful instrumental, as if to retrospectively disprove the famous review mentioned above, which noted that instrumentals had never been Everon's strong suit (a claim already contradicted at the time by the intro to "Venus" in 1997, as beautiful as anything by Dave Bainbridge), helps lighten the emotional load somewhat after bringing us to our knees. And Judith St�ber's enchanting voice on the ballad "Islanders" gently lifts us back up. And we stand tall as we listen to the glorious and energizing "Running", convinced that *North* is a truly ambitious album, a classic?and not just another heavy prog record?a formidable magnetic force that, while not reaching the absolute pinnacle of modern progressive rock, succeeds where so many others have failed, starting with Everon himself up to this point: to bring together in a single artistic work 10 crisp, simple, and clear melodies, set in 10 rings of precious metal, resting on 10 harmonic velvet cases. With the uncertain style of their early days having given way to a confident musical personality, Everon's music?that of their new album in particular?can fulfill the deepest progressive aspirations hidden within us. There's no doubt that *North* could give Everon the place it deserves: on the podium. At last!

items.body: Columbus’s Pinta, Niña and Santa María sail through “Delfín del Mundo” alongside pineapples, cockerels, chocolate, tobacco and caipirinhas, a roll call of conquest and tropical produce chanted over a psychedelic cumbia. “Delfín del Mundo” is the third and final single from Desertropical, the new EP from Dr. Rayo, due in October on Costa Rican label Lácteo Cósmico. The project belongs to Red Jesus, a Chilean-Mexican percussionist and producer who spent 2014 to 2020 on Mexico’s independent circuit. Now based in Madrid, he launched the project with a sold-out night at Moby Dick. Red Jesus made the track with Barzo, the San José-born DJ and producer who runs Lácteo Cósmico and has remixed Janelle Monáe and Erykah Badu. He came to Madrid for a short visit, and the pair recorded most of the instruments live at Dr. Rayo’s base. Barzo then built the electronic production on top of those takes. The earlier singles “Mexicali Tropical” and “Owl on Cocaine” opened big and dramatic, while “Delfín del Mundo” settles into a mid-tempo sway built on a slow-burning bassline, live percussion and a vocal delivered close to a chant. The vocal carries a message of pride in Latin American roots, and the cacao, tobacco and pineapples in the lyric were growing in the Americas long before Columbus’s ships arrived. Desertropical gets a launch party at Madrid’s Siroco at the end of September, with Spanish dates to follow in Seville, Oviedo, Gijón, Logroño and Santander. Stream “Delfín del Mundo” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Dr. Rayo x Barzo – Delfín del Mundo appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Eight tracks, two of them longer than eight minutes and one past eleven: Fields of the Nephilim built their third album around length. Beggars Banquet released “Elizium” on 24 September 1990, two years after “The Nephilim” had taken the gothic rock band from Stevenage to number 12 in the UK. The new album peaked at number 22. It turns 36 this year, and it remains the last studio record by the line-up of Carl McCoy, Tony Pettitt, Peter Yates, Paul Wright and Alexander “Nod” Wright. The band recorded “Elizium” in 1990 at Park Gate Studios in Battle, East Sussex, with additional recording and mixing at Astoria in Hampton Court. Andy Jackson, the engineer on Pink Floyd‘s late-1980s records, produced the album with the band and engineered the sessions; Jon Carin added keyboards. McCoy wrote the lyrics and the five members share the music credits. The title respells Elysium, the afterlife of Greek religion, and “At the Gates of Silent Memory” opens with the voice of Aleister Crowley reading from his poem “At Sea” in a 1920 recording. Beverley Carruthers shot the front sleeve, and Sheer Faith and Chris Bigg designed the packaging. ‘Elizium’ tracklist, singles and reissues The album runs 48 minutes and 3 seconds: “(Dead But Dreaming)”, “For Her Light”, “At the Gates of Silent Memory”, “(Paradise Regained)”, “Submission”, “Sumerland (What Dreams May Come)”, “Wail of Sumer” and “And There Will Your Heart Be Also”. Beggars Banquet issued it in the UK on LP, CD and cassette, with Rebel Rec. and SPV handling the German-speaking countries. “For Her Light” came out as the lead single in July 1990 and reached number 54 in the UK; “Sumerland (Dreamed Version)” followed in November 1990 and peaked at number 37. Music On Vinyl repressed the album on LP in 2011. Beggars Arkive marked the 30th anniversary on 11 December 2020 with a 180-gram dark green vinyl edition, and on 5 April 2024 released an expanded double LP on brick red vinyl. That edition spreads the album over three sides and adds four tracks on the fourth: “Sumerland (Single Version)”, “For Her Light (Two)”, “Submission Two (The Dub Posture)” and “Sumerland (Dreamed Version)”. John Dent handled the analogue transfer and Sean Magee cut the vinyl master. About Fields of the Nephilim Fields of the Nephilim formed in Stevenage, Hertfordshire, in 1984 around vocalist Carl McCoy, bassist Tony Pettitt, guitarist Paul Wright, drummer Alexander “Nod” Wright and saxophonist Gary Wisker. Peter Yates joined on guitar in 1985, the year the band released the “Burning the Fields” EP on its own Tower Release label. Jungle Records reissued it and financed the “Returning to Gehenna” EP in 1986. Situation Two, the Beggars Banquet imprint, signed the band in 1986 and released the singles “Power” and “Preacher Man” ahead of the debut album “Dawnrazor” in May 1987. The second album, “The Nephilim”, followed on 5 September 1988 and entered the UK chart at number 12, with “Moonchild” reaching number 28 as a single. The stand-alone single “Psychonaut” peaked at number 35 in May 1989, and the band moved up to the parent Beggars Banquet label for “Elizium” in September 1990. The two-night Festival of Fire at London’s Town & Country Club in 1991 produced the live album “Earth Inferno”, released on 25 March 1991, and the concert video “Visionary Heads”. McCoy left later that year. Pettitt, Yates and the Wright brothers continued as Rubicon with singer Andy Delaney, releasing “What Starts, Ends” in 1992 and “Room 101” in 1995, while McCoy formed Nefilim, whose only album “Zoon” appeared in 1996. McCoy and Pettitt announced a reunion at the Zillo Festival in Germany on 15 August 1998. Jungle Records issued the single “One More Nightmare (Trees Come Down)” in May 2000 and, in October 2002, the album “Fallen”, compiled from 1997 to 2001 recordings and disowned by the band as unauthorised. “Mourning Sun”, the first new Fields of the Nephilim studio album since “Elizium”, came out on 28 November 2005. A new line-up returned to the stage at the London Astoria in May 2007 and headlined M’era Luna in 2008. The double live album “Ceromonies (Ad Mortem Ad Vitam)”, recorded at Shepherd’s Bush Empire, appeared on McCoy’s Sacred Symphony label in April 2012, and the single “Prophecy” followed on 17 March 2016. Guitarist Tom Edwards, a member from 2008 to 2016, died in January 2017, as Side-Line reported in Fields of the Nephilim / Adam Ant guitarist Tom Edwards dies aged 41. Beggars Arkive has since reissued the Situation Two and Beggars Banquet catalogue: the 30th anniversary “Elizium” in December 2020, an expanded “The Nephilim” in October 2023, the four-track expanded “Elizium” in April 2024 and a remastered “Dawnrazor” in December 2025. McCoy and Pettitt lead the current line-up with guitarists Gavin King and Adam Leach. Thirty-six years after its release, “Elizium” closes the first chapter of that catalogue, the final album of the original five-piece before “Earth Inferno” documented its last shows.

items.body: Tanner McGraw sings and John Beckmann stays off the microphone on “Nothing Is Missing”, the third single from Utopia PKWY, out on 25 September 2026 with a video. Utopia PKWY is the new project of Beckmann, the New York songwriter and producer behind The Mortal Prophets, and the single precedes the project’s first album, “Debut”, due on 6 November 2026. Beckmann wrote and produced the track alone; McGraw takes the lead vocal and Lawson Mars adds backing vocals. Utopia PKWY mix post-pop hooks with synth-wave-tinged psychedelia, and bring keyboards, theremins and sitars into the arrangements. The single follows “I Knew You Would Be Trouble”, released on 3 July 2026, and “Sleep In Moving Colors”, released on 14 August 2026, both with official videos on the project’s YouTube channel. The “Nothing Is Missing” video was not yet public at the time of writing, so the player below carries the second single, whose video upload is titled “I Sleep In Moving Colors”. Beckmann described the new song as “Less a song than a philosophical hallucination, more like a midnight transmission from the far side of grief – where loss doesn’t disappear, it simply changes frequency and keeps humming beneath the skin.” The project takes its name from Utopia Parkway in Queens, the street where the Surrealist artist Joseph Cornell lived and worked. Beckmann calls McGraw and Mars, his two younger collaborators, the “kids in the neighborhood”. Both singers already appeared on the two most recent psychedelic dream-pop albums by The Mortal Prophets, and Utopia PKWY moves that line-up into brighter, more melodic songs. ‘Debut’ tracklist and release dates “Debut” runs to ten tracks: “I Knew You Were Trouble”, “Sleep In Moving Colors”, “Nothing Is Missing”, “If I Could Steal One More Kiss”, “You Talk Like Every Feeling”, “What Disappears”, “Come In Waves”, “Glitter And Doom”, “Fall Into You” and “Dreaming I’m A Rock Star”. The tracklist spells the opener “I Knew You Were Trouble”, while the single and its video carry the title “I Knew You Would Be Trouble”. The closing title also appears on The Mortal Prophets’ July 2026 album “Ain’t No Fool”. The earlier Utopia PKWY singles are on Spotify and Apple Music; the album page on the official site lists the release dates for all three singles and the album. About Utopia PKWY Utopia PKWY is the 2026 side project of John Beckmann, a New York singer, songwriter, producer and visual artist who has recorded as The Mortal Prophets since 2022. That project opened with the EP “Stomp The Devil” on 8 July 2022 and the album “Me And The Devil” on 9 December 2022, both built on reworked blues standards. “Dealey Plaza Blues” followed on 28 July 2023, the ambient guitar album “Guitarworks” on 22 December 2023, the EP “Sleeping In My Bed” on 15 March 2024, the opera “Hanussen: The Enigmatic Clairvoyant” on 15 April 2024, the EP “ICNCLST/” on 20 August 2024 and “Laurel Canyon – Lost Sessions (1966-69)” on 29 November 2024. In 2025 came “Ghost Land” (17 January), “French Summer” (16 May), “Guitarworks II” (28 July) and the covers EP “Under The Influence” (5 December). The move toward dream-pop and psychedelia began with “Hide Inside The Moon”, released on 2 January 2026, the first Mortal Prophets record with Tanner McGraw on lead vocals. “Not Here, Not There” followed on 3 April 2026 with McGraw and Lawson Mars sharing the vocals over synth-wave keyboards, theremins and sitars, and “Ain’t No Fool”, with Jake Burden on vocals, arrived on 3 July 2026. On the same day Beckmann launched Utopia PKWY with “I Knew You Would Be Trouble”, again with McGraw and Mars singing, and released “Sleep In Moving Colors” on 14 August 2026. “Nothing Is Missing” on 25 September 2026 is the last single before “Debut” on 6 November 2026.

items.body: Uboa releases the live album “Every Reactor Four a Friend (Live at Roadburn 2024)” through The Flenser on 22 September 2026, with a vinyl edition to follow as part of the label’s Membership Series 8 Exclusive. The three-track release is a recording of “Meltdown,” a piece Roadburn commissioned Uboa to compose for its 2024 edition. Uboa’s ‘Meltdown’ performance from Roadburn 2024 Roadburn commissioned Uboa to write two original works for its 2024 festival: “Calm Down,” a quieter piece, and its counterpart “Meltdown,” performed alongside TOomD’s “Shut Down.” “Every Reactor Four a Friend” is the live recording of “Meltdown,” captured from the mixing desk at Roadburn and later remixed and reworked, since some onboard vocal effects and microphones were missing from the available stems. The title refers to Reactor Four at Chernobyl, the reactor that melted down in the 1986 disaster. Musically, the release leans on power electronics and cut-up harsh noise, closer to the extremity of Uboa’s 2018 album “The Sky May Be” than the more intricate construction of her recent records. Uboa described the themes behind the performance directly: “It’s about embracing the overwhelm rather than shaming oneself for it. All the shame, anger and overwhelm was put in this short performance.” She added: “Sometimes it’s fine to just crash the fuck out. Sometimes it is necessary.” The album runs three tracks: “Dys,” “Do Not Comply In Advance” and “Ascension Threshold.” Every Reactor Four a Friend (Live at Roadburn 2024) by Uboa The Flenser also published a full-album stream of the performance: All Bandcamp proceeds from “Every Reactor Four a Friend” go toward covering Xandra’s gender-affirming surgery costs through 21 October 2026. About Uboa Uboa is a solo power electronics and noise project active since 2010, based in Melbourne, Australia. Early releases “Sometimes Light” (2010) and “Jouissance” (2013) were self-released before the 2018 album “The Sky May Be” arrived on the Australian label Art As Catharsis. “The Origin of My Depression” followed in 2019, initially self-released before The Flenser reissued it on vinyl after Uboa signed to the San Francisco label in February 2023. The Flenser then released the 2024 studio album “The Great Impossible Light,” featuring contributions from Blood of a Pomegranate, Otay:Onii, Charlie Looker and Haela Hunt-Hendrix of Liturgy. Uboa performed three sets at Roadburn Festival in Tilburg, Netherlands, in April 2024, including the live debut of “The Origin of My Depression” performed in full alongside the commissioned pieces “Calm Down” and “Meltdown.” “Every Reactor Four a Friend (Live at Roadburn 2024)” is the recording of that “Meltdown” performance, released through The Flenser two years on.

items.body: Berlin-based darkwave act Night Nail has released “Vile Train”, a gothic rock single that previews the band’s fourth studio album, Infinite Fountain, due November 6, 2026 through Icy Cold Records. The song arrives with an official video directed and edited by Jean De Oliviera. ‘Vile Train’ single details “Vile Train” was mixed and post-produced by William Faith at 13 Studio in Chicago, with co-production by Night Nail in Berlin and additional vocals and guitar from VV & the Void. Frontman Brandon Robert said the track drew its initial inspiration from a visit to Pompeii, where a fresco depicting an angel and a demon in an embrace suggested “dark and brutal truths about love sung in a twisted but beautiful way.” The video reunites the band with director Jean De Oliviera, whose previous work with Night Nail includes “Hollow Day,” “Little Armenia” and “Narcoleptic Dream Catcher.” Shot in black and white, it cuts between Robert and bassist Ilija Gavrilenko performing among amplifiers and outdoor scenes set among stone arches and fountain basins. A full tracklist for Infinite Fountain has not been announced. The album also includes mixing and post-production work by Sven Wolff of Patenbrigade: Wolff. Night Nail plans to support the release with shows across the US, UK and Europe during 2026 and 2027. About Night Nail Night Nail formed in Los Angeles in 2013 and relocated to Berlin in 2018, the same year the band’s debut album, LA Demons, appeared on Cleopatra Records. March To Autumn followed in 2020 through Cold Transmission, and Fates Explained arrived on Metropolis Records in 2023, mixed and mastered by Pete Burns of Kill Shelter; Side-Line covered the single “Fates Explained” at the time. The band followed with the archival release Early Demons and Demos and the remix album Fates Remade in 2024, after earlier singles including “Narcoleptic Dream Catcher” and “Cracks In My Heart”, the latter featuring Luna De La Torre on vocals. Night Nail’s catalogue connects darkwave electronics with gothic rock’s appetite for emotional extremes, a combination built up over four albums and multiple labels since the band’s Los Angeles beginnings. “Vile Train” and the forthcoming Infinite Fountain, out on Icy Cold Records, mark the band’s next chapter and its first full-length since 2023’s Fates Explained. Follow Night Nail: – Bandcamp – Spotify – Website

Both listings are running through the band’s official shop and close at midnight CEST on 27 September 2026. IAMX tour dates for 2026 and 2027 23 September 2026 – Oslo, Norway – John Dee 24 September 2026 – Malmö, Sweden – Plan B 25 September 2026 – Helsinki, Finland – On The Rocks, with Aux Animaux 13 November 2026 – Santiago, Chile – Santiago Gothic Treffen 14 November 2026 – São Paulo, Brazil – Madame Club 24-25 July 2027 – Cologne, Germany – Amphi Festival 31 July – 1 August 2027 – Thale, Germany – Unter dem Himmel About IAMX IAMX is the solo project of British musician Chris Corner, who co-founded the trip-hop group Sneaker Pimps in Hartlepool in 1994. After a fourth Sneaker Pimps album went unreleased, Corner kept the songs, moved to London and released them as the debut album “Kiss + Swallow” in 2004. Later albums include “The Alternative” (2006), “Kingdom of Welcome Addiction” (2009), “Volatile Times” (2011), “The Unified Field” (2013), “Metanoia” (2015), “Unfall” (2017), “Alive In New Light” (2018), the acoustic rework album “Echo Echo” (2020) and “Machinate” (2021), followed by “Fault Lines¹” (2023) and “Fault Lines²” (2024). IAMX opened 2026 with the single “Artificial Innocence” ahead of a European tour, and Corner discussed his songwriting approach in a Side-Line interview in May. Gözde Düzer, who tours with the band on bass and theremin and records on her own as Aux Animaux from Stockholm, spoke to Side-Line in March about joining the IAMX live band and touring with Chris Corner. The “Recollections” tour has since carried the band through Scandinavia this week, with dates in Chile and Brazil to follow in November and festival shows at Amphi Festival and Unter dem Himmel booked for the summer of 2027. This week’s silent auction of stage props from the tour runs alongside that live schedule.
