items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — D'Arcansiel, an Italian band with a French comically misspelled name (all the more strange given that the opening track of their 1988 debut album is aptly titled "Un Arc dans le Ciel"), which emerged in the mid-1980s and disbanded a few years later, we were familiar with their three neo-prog albums (including the quite respectable *Still Searching*, released in 1990), heavily influenced by Marillion from the same era, though none of them left a lasting impression on our minds, already saturated with prog masterpieces of all kinds. Suffice it to say, I wouldn't have bet much on a new Arcansiel album ? I would have been wrong, because that's exactly what just happened with *Hard Times*, an undeniable success in a very personal RPI style that easily makes you forget the band's earlier efforts. This proves once again, as the saying goes, that it's never too late to do things right. "Too Late!" Yet this is the painful cry of alarm delivered?through the voice of the excellent singer Marco Leccese and the band's new keyboardist Davide Sorella?right from the introduction of the first track, a nearly 18-minute suite that Sorella wrote and composed.The state of Planet Earth is cause for concern, and even if it's not certain that the point of no return has been reached, we can safely say that we will not leave this place in the same condition we found it. The beauty of the world is fragile, and humankind is a malevolent shadow that has never ceased to wither it away. Progress continues its rapid march regardless of the circumstances and seems to defy even the most alarming signs. So is it too late to avert disaster? Sorella tells us instead that it's too late to keep wasting our time making bad decisions or failing to take any serious action.Musically, "Too Late" is a grand symphonic prog epic as captivating and inexhaustible as the theme it explores. With a neo-Baroque-inspired leitmotif that gives center stage to a keyboard-dominated instrumental section (a commanding synth, a very assertive piano, a mischievous harpsichord, and a swift Hammond organ playing in rondo form), all in service of hyper-melodic vocal parts?reminiscent of what Oliviero Lacagnina has recently done with The Samurai of Prog, or even Gryphon at their most prog?this majestic epic manages to bathe discreetly in a fluid, slightly jazzy atmosphere, then bursts into a symphony that is more melancholic than desperate, at times bordering on the tragic. After such a fireworks display?18 minutes that seem to fly by in the blink of an eye and that one wishes could last an eternity?the rest might seem to take a back seat, less grandiose. But this impression quickly fades upon listening to the next three tracks, which are just as brilliant."Hard Times" (like the title of Dickens' novel), can be understood as "Difficult Times" but 'Hard' also means "Tough." We are indeed living in an era with problems that are difficult (but not impossible?) to solve on every level (social, cultural, ethical, ecological, political?); but we are also in a world that is hard to live in for many of us?and that "us" encompasses the majority of living beings. Arcansiel's album offers us some enlightening accounts of this. From the scathing and mocking "Puppets and Puppeteers" (a description of one of the most irritating aspects of new media) to the disillusioned "Heaven Is Not Here" (beware of smooth talkers and false promises), the social issues addressed in *Hard Times* are critical reflections that remain relevant and never fail to move the listener.The result of a collaboration between bassist Felice Lombardo and guitarist Sebastiano Valvo, "Puppets and Puppeteers " (7:51) brings a fairly distinct shift in musical atmosphere by adopting a deliberate tempo with irregular measures in a powerful neo-prog style reminiscent of early Asgard (Leccese's vocals play a part in this), illuminated by dazzling synth solos that readily give way to a magnificent lyrical guitar solo. "Heaven Is Not Here" (11:22), written by the bassist, also offers remarkable moments, especially for those who appreciate Jon Anderson's more peaceful work paired with Genesis's "Supper's Ready."Personally, I have a soft spot for the unpredictable "My Old Same Mistakes" (7:27), written by the duo Sorella and Valvo in a melodic style quite similar to the romantic, post-Gabriel era of Genesis, and in which Marco Leccese once again works wonders (his "Save Me," sung with great conviction, is sure to be memorable), though the second half?following a medieval-influenced instrumental bridge?leans toward a swaying jazz-rock style, before concluding with Canterbury-style prog, all seamlessly strung together. As surprising as it is delightful.More than 30 years have passed since *Still Searching*, and only drummer Gianni Lavagno remains to ensure the band's continuity and the legitimacy of the Arcansiel name, though he did not participate in writing the songs for *Hard Times*. The compositions penned by the other three musicians?evolving into a sort of shimmering neo-prog with a distinctly Italian sensibility, featuring numerous twists, breaks, and inspired resurgences?are far richer and more diverse than those of the original Arcansiel. Reusing the same name may seem like a questionable choice, even an abuse of the name. But after all, the label on the bottle isn't very important when it contains such nectar?to be savored without moderation to make our lives sweeter.

items.body: Review by Rysiek P. — An opportunity like this certainly cannot be overlooked. Twenty years after releasing their debut album, *Armed Forces of Simantipak*, the band Khatsaturjan?whose name derives from the renowned Armenian composer Aram Khachaturian?has released a new record titled *Monolog Chronosa*. Their discography also includes two other albums - *Disconcerto Grosso* (2010) and *Beast, Machine & Man* (2015) - and their history is notable for the fact that, as early as their 2002 debut single *Aramsome Sums*, they performed their own "rock" versions of Modest Mussorgsky's *Night on Bald Mountain* and Hector Berlioz's *March to the Scaffold*. All of this was presented in progressive hard-rock arrangements that incorporated elements reminiscent of the band Gentle Giant. Furthermore, critics hailed the group's first album as a benchmark for symphonic rock. One might pessimistically remark, "But that was years ago". Yet, it is certainly worth checking out where Khatsaturjan stands today. The band's latest release comprises forty-seven minutes of music spread across seven tracks, with an album title suggesting that the passage of time is the central theme. This phenomenon is observed and described from various perspectives - including, perhaps most importantly, the human condition and the personal, often highly subjective experience of life passing by. The title of the opening track - "Lessons (On Human Obsolescence)" - gives one food for thought right from the start. However, do not expect dark, atmospheric arrangements here. The composition is remarkably balanced,almost conservative in its playing style and employs familiar progressive rock tropes, with one notable exception: a strong emphasis on vocal polyphony (a true hallmark of this album) and a more prominent role for keyboards. These two elements define the musical structure of the song, which opens with the sound of a bell before embarking on a progressive journey rich in engaging tempo shifts and instrumental virtuosity. The second track, "What Was True," takes a slightly different approach. Here, the band clearly leans toward a modern progressive sound, successfully utilizing "new textures" to craft a unique atmosphere that straddles the line between atmospheric progressive rock (or even neo-prog) and a vocal-harmony-driven ballad. Once again, vocal polyphony and synthesizers serve as the building blocks for both this specific track and the album as a whole. The track "The Dystopian Spirit Of Club Energy" also features a piano-and-synthesizer-driven sound. Yet, in this composition, the band draws upon classical music and classical time signatures. The piano sets the arrangement's course, serving as a backdrop for highly impressive vocal performances. Only halfway through does the track remind us that it is 2026, showing how a guitar-driven rhythmic boost can yield a truly successful result. Incorporating electronic elements into the arrangement only enhances the musical value of this piece, which runs over five minutes in length. It was only while listening to "Song Of Days" that I realized what truly draws me to the band's music: a delicacy and almost theatrical storytelling style, skillfully blended with classical influences, alongside magnificent tales sung with a masterful, gradual build-up of vocal intensity. With a full arsenal of musical tools at their disposal, Khatsaturjan selects only those that fit the symphonic-progressive narrative, all while keeping classical music traditions close at hand. "Song Of Days" is a perfect example of this approach. It makes brilliant use of symphonic arrangements, blending them with flawless vocal lines and weaving in thoroughly modern progressive guitar motifs to create a truly well-crafted track. "DID Memoir" shares a similar, song-oriented character. It opens with a "classic" sense of grandeur, progressive guitar work, and... such delicate vocals. Everything weaves together into a structure that challenges the listener - filled with improvisational passages that hark back to classical music and, as an added bonus, theatrical farce-style interludes appearing midway through the fourth minute. Just listen closely around the five-minute mark for a dose of rap; this element, yet another instance of the piece's stylistic multiplicity, is entirely justified given the title: "DID Memoir." While the acronym refers to Dissociative Identity Disorder, it also serves as a fitting title for the track's eclectic, multi-stylistic nature. Following a symphonic opening, the penultimate track on this magnificent album - "The Keepers of the Philosopher's Stone" - simply sends shivers down the spine with its superb vocal lines. It features backing vocals, humming passages, and a lead vocal that stands out tonally, its rough timbre lending an air of deep mystery. Yet, what makes this composition truly exceptional is the extensive and successful incorporation of motifs drawn from classical music; the violin sounds and classical time signatures transform this five-plus-minute piece into a remarkable puzzle of motifs and an intricate arrangement. A madrigal-like character, blended with thoroughly modern synthesizer and guitar sounds, seems to elevate the track's central theme - fittingly so for a song about the "Philosopher's Stone," which here truly transmutes individual notes into "gold." With this release, the end comes all too soon. Were it not for the fact that the closing track - "Mundus Meus (This World of Mine)" - employs every possible device to captivate the listener from the very first note, one might feel that the magnificent preceding track left something musically unresolved, a void that could neither be filled nor replaced. "Mundus Meus..." stands as a magnificent anthem and the perfect culmination of the album; the Latin lyrics sound both prophetic and majestic without detracting from the depth of the message. And although the track features numerous gentle prog-metal solos, it remains, at its core, a thoroughly symphonic-progressive composition. If I say that I am very - truly very - pleasantly surprised by the latest work from the group Khatsaturjan, is that recommendation enough? If not, I'll add that the band features essentially the same lineup as on their debut and subsequent albums, even though musical light-years have passed since that first release (in 2002). Atte Kurri (vocals, bass, keyboards), Ilkka Piispala (vocals, drums, keyboards, bass), and Ilkka Saarikivi (vocals, keyboards, bass, violin) continue to demonstrate that musical trends don't matter to them. It is significant that Khatsaturjan is a group of friends who get together only when they want to record something; they are not a band that makes a living from touring and recording albums. On their Facebook page, the band writes: "We work slowly because Khatsaturjan is not our profession - it is a passion project and a beloved hobby. Whenever we decide to work on a new album, we know a years-long effort lies ahead, with no financial reward whatsoever. Yet, time and again, we take on new projects." Perhaps this approach allows them to maintain a sense of detachment and find the tranquility needed to create new music? You surely know that things tend to flow more easily when there are no deadlines hanging over your head. And since we will likely have to wait a long time for the next sign of musical life from Khatsaturjan, we should simply enjoy this highly successful release - one that has earned a spot in my top ten albums of the year.

items.album: die Jimi-Hendrix-Erfahrung
items.excerpt: 24. September, vor 60 Jahren. Jimi Hendrix landet in London. 24 Jahre alt, in seiner Heimat USA ein Nobody. In London aber ist Hendrix schnell eine Sensation. items.body: 24. September, vor 60 Jahren. Jimi Hendrix landet in London. 24 Jahre alt, in seiner Heimat USA ein Nobody. In London aber ist Hendrix schnell eine Sensation. Spielerisch, kompositorisch; die Breaks und Arrangements, die Show, die Ausstrahlung, Afro-Aura, das Wie. Wie er die Gitarre behandelte, misshandelte, keine Töne spielte, sondern fühlte und weiterhauchte, Akkorde und Noten ineinander verkuppelte wie in einem wild zerrupften Kingsize-Bett. Hoch-konzentriert und dann wie ein aus einem Wanderzirkus flüchtender 5-jähriger.Keine vier Jahre später, am 18. September 1970,  wird Hendrix’ – vermutlich – kaum mehr lebender Körper vom Samarkand Hotel zum St. Mary Abbots Hospital gebracht, wo der diensthabende Notfallarzt nach Wiederbelebungsmaßnahmen um 12:45 Uhr den Tod des Amerikaners feststellt. So weit, was wie Fakten klingt.   Im HHV Shop kaufenThe Jimi Hendrix ExperienceAre You Experiencedab 24.99€Jimi HendrixMagic Boy: The Jimi Hendrix Experience Live At Berkeley First Showab 34.99€The Jimi Hendrix ExperienceWinterlandab 31.99€Jimi HendrixElectric Ladyland 50th Anniversary Deluxe Editionab 104.99€Die Platten von Jimi Hendrix findest du im HHV-Shop Geil und aufregend Daten sind ja viel wert. Zahlen auch. Selbst wenn man genau darüber das Phänomen Jimi Hendrix am allerwenigsten erfasst, über das Messbare. Ausweislich der Plattenverkäufe in den USA (RIAA Buchführung) kommen Hendrix‘ drei zu Lebzeiten aufgenommenen Studioalben auf 10 Millionen; alleine Thriller wird mit Mio. 34 gelistet, Hotel California mit 28 Mio., Back in Black mit 27 Mio., Led Zeppelin IV mit 24 Mio., The Wall mit 23 Mio. Hendrix hat seinen Status als Legende nicht wegen der Zahlen inne. Zurück ins Jahr 1966. Die neu gegründeten Cream machten als Trio den aus den USA importierten Blues rockiger, auch – analog zu Jazz – anspruchsvoller. Fast sophisticated. Und während es bei Elvis, Beat und Pop um 7“-Singles, schnelllebiges Zeug zum Mitpfeifen und Vergessen ging, kam nun die Langspielplatte. Beatles‘ Revolver zerschoss Karrierekorsetts des alten Musters. Farbe fand ins Fernsehen. Das Raumschiff Enterprise hob ab; Jane Fonda ging weiter: sie sauste in Barbarella mit Stones-Muse Anita Pallenberg und Marcel Marceau ins Jahr 40.000. Die Zukunft, alles Kommende war noch geil und aufregend, voller Möglichkeiten. Die Sinne der Massen sensibilisiert, kam 1967 Beatles‘ Sgt. Peppers mit Klappcover. Das Album als Gesamtkunstwerk. Wie ein ausgerollter roter Teppich für Hendrix‘ Debüt Are You Experienced?. Das Album erschien im Mai 1967. Kein Jahr nach seiner Ankunft in London also. Wo er Tage nach seiner Landung noch in Clubs jammte, dann Vorgruppe für Cream spielte, gefolgt von mehreren Dates in Frankreich und der Münchner Diskothek Big Apple. Zu Pfingsten war er Headliner in Berlin. Zum Preis von drei Schachteln Zigaretten, DM 6,– Eintritt, im Vorverkauf.  »Einmaliges Sondergastspiel, Jimmy Hendrix mit The Experience aus London«. Einer Zeitzeugin zufolge, Absolventin der Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics, verliefen sich, fußläufig vom Club Neue Welt, mehrere Besuchende – unter ihnen der 68er-Kult-Autor Bernward Vesper mit seiner Lebensgefährtin Gudrun Ensslin in der Hasenheide. Tagelang. Der Beginn des Spektakels Inzwischen tritt Hendrix eigentlich nonstop auf, auch in den USA, auch mit The Who, im Package mit Cat Stevens, spielte um die 400 Mal, an manchem Tag auch zwei Gigs. Parallel nahm Hendrix‘ Trio weiter im Studio auf. Mit mobilen Endgeräten, mitnehmbaren Schallplattenspieler, der es ihm erlaubte, drei Tage nach dem bahnbrechenden Beatles-Album den Titelsong zu spielen. Spieltechnik ständig am Reifen, aber auch die Technik, die das Massenphänomen begleitet. Sichtbar ist, dass er sich früh Boxen der P.A.-Firma WEM auf die Bühne stellt, die im Heavy Metal heute normativen Marshall-Türme ordert er bei Jim Marshall, dem ehemaligen Lehrer des Experience-Drummers Mitch Mitchell.   Das alles – Musik voller Energie und Lärm und nuancierten Gänsehautmomenten – vor kontinuierlich größeren Zuschauermengen. Explosiv und aufflammend im Finale bei Monterey Pop (dem ersten Baby des Summer of Love), abgeklärter und überwältigt kulminierend in Woodstock, wo Hendrix als Haupt-Attraktion auftrat. Für 500.000 in Woodstock wurde die Soundanlage fürs Publikum unglaublich professionalisiert. Um die 10.000 bis 12.000 Watt auf 16 Lautsprecher-Türmen, Speaker separat ausgerichtet auf die nahestehenden und die entfernteren Fans. Verantwortlich zeichnete sich der Mann, der beim Newport Jazz Festival am Mischpult stand, als die Jünger Bob Dylan ausbuhten, weil er zur E-Gitarre gewechselt war. Small world. Im Grunde war das, fand man später, die Blaupause für Mega-Spektakel-Events, der Übergang vom Beat-Treiben hin zum Big Business, speziell mit Solokünstlern, die sich leichter lenken lassen als Bands. Und die Person Hendrix, zwischen all dem? Charmanter Talker, schüchtern, charismatisch. Voller Gegensätze. Wie die ultra-krachenden Attacken neben Arrangements, flüssig wie ein Bach. Zudem war er offenbar ein Intensiv-Zuhörer, der analysierte, sofort nachahmte, was es wert war, mitgenommen zu werden; der verbesserte und alles lauter und elektrifiziert zurechtstutzte – wie in Unterhaltungen jeder Gitarrismus-Gitarrist herausfand. Ähnlich äußerten sich auch Joni Mitchell, Frank Zappa, Bob Dylan, Beatles, Pete Townshend. Schnell in der Auffassung, polyamourös mit Hörgewohnheiten. Voll da. Verstärker und Technik, Effekte und Astraltheorien, alles gleich aus den Vollen gekippt. So viel wie Hendrix verdiente zu der Zeit kein Musiker, auch keine Band, auch nicht Dylan oder Elvis. Kohle beiseitelegen oder unterschlagen konnten bis zu vier Manager gleichzeitig. Hendrix war umgarnt von Abstaubern und Nachtfaltern, Alles-Checkern und Blutegeln. Die Gitarre brennt ja sowie schon Knapp nach seinem 56.–Todestag – 18. September – kommentiert irgendwer auf YouTube: »Einfach absolut erstaunlich: Er starb 1970 und schuf in seinem kurzen Leben über 170 Songs – und hier sind wir im Jahr 2026, und Jimmy ist immer noch unerreicht. Sein Werk und sein Können waren ein wahres Meisterstück. Er verließ diese Welt als geliebter Mensch, und sein Schaffen wurde gut bewahrt. Seiner Eigenheiten war er sich bewusst und spannte die Saiten seiner Gitarre deshalb ganz bewusst verkehrt herum auf – damit auch lange nach seinem Tod niemand seine Musik Note für Note nachspielen oder kopieren könnte. Das wird niemals geschehen. Ruhe in Frieden, James Marshall Hendrix; du warst ein unglaublich begabter Mann.« 1970 drückte man das anders aus. Tony Palmer in electric revolution. Die Inside-Story der Pop-Stars1: »Jimi Hendrix spielte seine 240 V Gitarre mit den Zähnen, auf dem Rücken oder unterm Bein. Je nach Laune zertöpperte er sie oder steckte sie in Brand.« Geradezu ikonographischer Moment in der Geschichte des Rock als Pop: die weiße Strat in Flammen und daraufhin Anlass für Besucher und Glotzer, nach Monterey-Fanal nur darauf zu warten: wann spielt er die Saiten mit der Zunge, wann zerkloppt er die Klampfe, oder darf man erleben, dass er sie anzündet? Eine Nummernrevue, die vom Eigentlichen ablenkte. Frust.  Trotzdem, jetzt mal kurz: Die Finger verbrannte er sich im London Astoria (31. März 1967), in Monterey verfeuerte er »Wild Thing« (18. Juni 1967), bei Frank Zappa landeten irgendwann die Überreste einer beim Miami Pop Festival entflammten Stratocaster (19. Mai 1968).  Aber das Ding war, er war so ein krasser Gitarrist, dass… dass das allein schon genug war. Echt genug. Und der Showkram lenkte davon ab. Lou Reed »Er spielte ja rund um die Uhr«, erinnert Lou Reed, dessen Karriere mit Velvet Underground – selbe Zeit, selber Ort Greenwich Village – via Andy Warhol einen Schub bekam. »Seine Musik fand ich unterhaltsam, ebenso seine Show. Aber das Ding war, er war so ein krasser Gitarrist, dass… dass das allein schon genug war. Echt genug. Und der Showkram lenkte davon ab. Ich denke, das wurde ihm auch klar, und er wollte davon weg. Damit die Leute einfach auf die Musik achten. Unendlich viel hätte er noch bringen können. Aber die Situation, in der er eingeklemmt war… durch… entweder seine Plattenfirma, das Management, Konzertpromoter, die Publicity-Leute, dieser ganze Haufen Leute, mit denen man da zu tun hat. Die alle sagen ›Hey Jimi, wir haben doch diese Tour und du musst da, dort, da und dort und dort auch noch sein, so und so viele Leute kommen nicht rein, du solltest besser dies und das tun, dein Kontostand rutscht runter auf X, du willst Electric Ladyland [Studio] aufbauen und betreiben… vielleicht haut das nicht hin. Da lastete viel Druck auf ihm.«  Noch lange nicht ausgebrannt Was bleibt, sind die vier Jahre. Dazwischen Entfernungen und Grenzen und Stress, bei dem man schnell nicht mehr mitkriegt, wo oder warum man aufwacht. Is it tomorrow, or just the end of time? Und es bleiben drei offiziell abgenickte Studioalben. Mit rückwärts laufenden Tonbändern, Cartoon-ähnlichen Intros; und mit, generell ziemlich wenig beachtet: wahnsinnig berührenden Lyrics. Der essenzielle Punkt: Synästhesie, Comics oder Science-Fiction-Romane transferiert in Musik. Stimmungen. Lila Nebel als Gemütszustand, aber dabei eine hörbare Haltung. Das Ende war unnötig. Er hatte Pläne mit Miles Davis, liebelte mit Händel, Bach und dem ›Marsch‹ aus Tschaikowskis Nussknacker. Wollte sich in seinem Studio Electric Ladyland – wie die Beatles nach 1966 – nur noch dem Aufnehmen widmen. Da war noch so viel, da blieb noch so viel, was man mal machen müsste. Stattdessen wurden einige, nach seinem Tod und ohne sein Protestieren, sehr reich. In den ersten Nachrufen starb er mit 24. Andere spekulierten, er müsse ausgebrannt gewesen sein, nach so viel Drogen, so viel Exzess und Erfolg und Frauen und schlaflosen Nächten. John Mayall intonierte den Tod als unbeabsichtigte Überdosis2. Kleben blieb das Verdikt »nach neun Schlaftabletten an Erbrochenem erstickt … durch Selbstmord oder einen Unglücksfall« (Der Spiegel 31/1974). Das Nachspiel war ziemlich grässlich. Irre sponnen abartige Theorien.  Eric Burdon, der noch am 17. September mit Hendrix bei Ronnie Scott‘s Jazz Club jammte: »Er wirkte immer wie ein Geist, so gespenster-mäßig, er ließ niemanden an sich heran. Das Leben berührte er nur – das war sein Geheimnis –, an sich gerissen hat er nie irgendwas oder irgendwen.«   1 Tony Palmer: electric revolution. Die Inside Story der Pop-Stars, aus dem Englischen von Klaus Budzinski. Verlag Bärmeier & Nikel, Frankfurt/Main.2 »Accidental Suicide« auf John Mayall: Back to The Roots, Polydor 1971.

items.body: A centuries-old devotional song from Morocco’s Gnawa repertoire, “M’Bara Meskin” tells of poor M’Bara, left outside the shrine in torn clothes to brew his tea from leaves others have thrown away. Inside, the Sidi and the Lalla, Moroccan honorifics for a gentleman and a lady, sip theirs in their slippers. Sydney-born multi-instrumentalist Julian Belbachir has rebuilt it on reggae and dub, keeping the vocal in Moroccan Arabic, from sessions in Morocco, Mali, Australia, Canada and Jamaica. Belbachir was born to a Moroccan father and an Australian mother and grew up in Surry Hills and Redfern, where he started on West African drums at five under griots and master drummers from Sydney’s African diaspora. He went on to study percussion and instrument-making in Guinea, Senegal, Mali and Morocco, and plays the kamele n’goni, the harp-lute of Mali’s Wassoulou region. From 2013 to 2022 he drummed for the Australian Indigenous dub band OKA, and after the death of its founder, Stuart “Boga” Fergie, he went solo with his 2022 debut album, Babdoukkala. Gnawa music was carried into Morocco by West Africans brought north across the Sahara, many of them enslaved, and the personnel on his forthcoming album, The Golden Light, follow the same route: more than 30 musicians from Mali and Morocco, among them Moussa Diakite, lead guitarist for Salif Keita. “M’Bara Meskin” came out on 11 September as its first single, with the album due in February 2027. Belbachir hears the song as a portrait of “the hardships musicians face in their daily lives“. The video, shot on Super 8 over two trips to Essaouira three years apart, follows his collaborators through rehearsals, recording sessions and time with their community in the Atlantic port best known for its annual Gnawa festival. items.body: The Cult released their fifth studio album, “Ceremony,” on 23 September 1991, through Beggars Banquet in the United Kingdom and Sire in the United States. The English rock band, who had started the decade before as the post-punk groups Southern Death Cult and Death Cult, made the record as a two-piece with session players. It turns 35 this year. By the time the sessions began, the touring line-up had gone. Bassist Jamie Stewart retired and moved to Canada after the final leg of the “Sonic Temple” tour in April 1990, and drummer Matt Sorum left to join Guns N’ Roses, leaving vocalist Ian Astbury and guitarist Billy Duffy as the only official members. Todd Hoffman played bass and James Kottak drums on the demos. For the album itself, Mickey Curry returned on drums after his session work on “Sonic Temple,” with Charley Drayton on bass. Richie Zito produced, with Astbury and Duffy co-producing, and also contributed keyboards and harmonium. Benmont Tench played organ, piano and mellotron, Scott Thurston added synthesizer and piano to “If,” Suzie Katayama played cello on “Indian,” and Alex Acuña handled percussion on “Indian” and “Wonderland.” Tommy Funderburk sang backing vocals across most of the record, joined by Donny Gerrard, Mona Lisa and Yvonne St. James on “Sweet Salvation.” Phil Kaffel engineered, Mike Fraser mixed, and George Marino mastered the album at Sterling Sound in New York. Pre-production ran at Oliver Ferrand Studio in Los Angeles and Mates in North Hollywood, with recording at Music Grinder Studios in Hollywood and recording and mixing at A&M Recording Studios. The eleven tracks run 63 minutes and 38 seconds: “Ceremony,” “Wild Hearted Son,” “Earth Mofo,” “White,” “If,” “Full Tilt,” “Heart of Soul,” “Bangkok Rain,” “Indian,” “Sweet Salvation” and “Wonderland.” Astbury and Duffy wrote all of them. “Wild Hearted Son” opens with an excerpt from “The Grass Dance” performed by The American Indian Dance Theatre, and “White” quotes Lawrence Lipton’s 1959 book “The Holy Barbarians,” which Astbury took as the name of his next band in 1996. “Wild Hearted Son” was the first single, followed by “Heart of Soul” in 1992. “White” appeared as a single in Canada only, “Sweet Salvation” was issued in Argentina in 1992 as “Dulce Salvación,” and the title track came out as a promotional single in Spain. The cover photograph, taken by John Running, drew a lawsuit. The parents of the Native American boy pictured on the sleeve sued over the unauthorised use of their son’s image, a case Entertainment Weekly reported on 19 June 1992. The New York proceedings against Warner Bros. Records were dismissed in February 1997 for lack of personal jurisdiction; a separate action filed in the District Court of South Dakota on 10 April 1995 was terminated on 16 May 1995. The dispute held up the record’s release in several territories, with South Korea and Thailand not seeing it until 1992 and Turkey not until the band played Istanbul in June 1993. Alan Forbes handled the art direction and design with the band. “Ceremony” reached number 9 on the UK albums chart, was certified gold by the BPI, and went platinum in Canada. Sources differ on its US peak: Wikipedia’s entry on the album gives number 25 on the Billboard 200, while its entry on the band gives number 34. The Ceremonial Stomp tour took the record through Europe in 1991 and North America in 1992, with Michael Lee on drums, Kinley “Barney” Wolfe on bass and John Sinclair on keyboards. The album streams on Spotify. About The Cult Ian Astbury formed Southern Death Cult in Bradford, Yorkshire, in 1981, with guitarist Buzz Burrows, bassist Barry Jepson and drummer Aki Nawaz Qureshi. They played their first show at the Queen’s Hall in Bradford on 29 October 1981, signed to Situation Two, an offshoot of Beggars Banquet, and released the triple A-side single “Moya” in 1982 before ending after sixteen months with a final Manchester show in February 1983. Jepson went on to co-found Into A Circle with Paul “Bee” Hampshire in 1985. In April 1983 Astbury teamed up with Billy Duffy, who had played in the Nosebleeds alongside Morrissey, then Lonesome No More and Theatre of Hate. The new band, Death Cult, added bassist Jamie Stewart and drummer Raymond Taylor Smith, later known as Ray Mondo, both from the London post-punk group Ritual. Death Cult debuted live in Oslo on 25 July 1983 and released the “Death Cult” EP the same month, with the “Gods Zoo” single following in October. Nigel Preston, previously of Sex Gang Children, replaced Mondo that September. The group shortened its name to The Cult in January 1984, ahead of an appearance on the Channel 4 programme The Tube. “Dreamtime,” recorded at Rockfield Studios in Monmouth with producer John Brand, arrived in September 1984 and reached number 21 in the UK. Preston was dismissed in June 1985 and Big Country’s Mark Brzezicki played the “Love” sessions that July and August; the Steve Brown-produced album reached number 4. Les Warner drummed on the world tour that ran from late September 1985 to June 1986. The follow-up was first recorded as “Peace” with Brown at the Manor Studios in Oxfordshire, then re-cut in New York with Rick Rubin and issued in April 1987 as “Electric,” which also reached number 4. Kid Chaos joined on bass for that tour, with Stewart moving to rhythm guitar. “Sonic Temple,” produced by Bob Rock and recorded in Vancouver between October and December 1988, followed in April 1989 and went gold in the UK and platinum in the US. After “Ceremony,” Astbury and Duffy replaced the touring band in 1993 with Craig Adams of The Mission and drummer Scott Garrett, the line-up that recorded “The Cult” with Bob Rock in October 1994. The band split in March 1995 during a South American tour. Astbury formed Holy Barbarians, whose only album “Cream” came out in May 1996, and released the solo record “Spirit\Light\Speed” in June 2000. Duffy worked with Coloursound alongside Craig Adams and Mike Peters, then Dead Men Walking and Cardboard Vampyres. The Cult reformed in 1999 with Sorum and bassist Martyn LeNoble, signed to Atlantic for “Beyond Good and Evil” in 2001, and went on ice again in late 2002. Astbury spent that second break fronting the surviving members of The Doors in a group billed variously as The Doors of the 21st Century, D21c and Riders on the Storm. He announced his departure in February 2007, stating: “I have decided to move on and focus on my own music and legacy.” The Cult had already reunited in January 2006 with drummer John Tempesta, guitarist Mike Dimkich and bassist Chris Wyse. “Born into This,” produced by Martin “Youth” Glover of Killing Joke, came out on Roadrunner on 16 October 2007. Cooking Vinyl signed the band in May 2011 and released “Choice of Weapon” on 22 May 2012 and “Hidden City” on 5 February 2016, both produced by Rock. James Stevenson replaced Dimkich on rhythm guitar in 2013 and Grant Fitzpatrick replaced Wyse on bass in 2015. Duffy also appeared on Wayne Hussey’s 2020 charity remake of “Tower of Strength,” alongside members of Depeche Mode, The Smiths, The Mission, Gary Numan, etc.. The band signed to Black Hill Records in May 2020, began recording at Rockfield in August 2020 with producer Tom Dalgety, and released “Under the Midnight Sun” on 7 October 2022 with Charlie Jones on bass. On 23 October 2025 the group announced a touring hiatus of undetermined length to concentrate on writing and recording. “Ceremony,” the only album in that catalogue made without a settled line-up, turns 35 this year.

items.body: The German duo Grimoire De Occulte has been active for several years now and has released the majority of its work, particularly in recent years. Inspired by Bernd Hermanns, aka ‘Baal’ (owner of Dunkelheit Produktionen and also active in several other projects), and ‘Philosoph’, they originally released this album in 2025, with the CD version following this year. The title word ‘Ajna’ undoubtedly refers to the Sanskrit word usually translated as ‘perceiving’, ‘knowing’, or ‘insight’. It also represents the sixth chakra, which is associated with the so-called third eye. This aligns perfectly with the approach of this project, which has always been closely linked to ritual and mysticism. We are presented with an elaborate and unique track lasting nearly 40 minutes. “Ajna: Transmissions” invites the listener to immerse themselves in an esoteric world in which the ‘other side’ plays a prominent role. This naturally provides inspiration for a dark composition, with the duo presenting us with a persistent, ominous wave of sound. At first glance, it may seem somewhat monotonous, yet the composition is enriched with humming sound effects and additional sounds, including all kinds of crackling field recordings. The whole piece is also punctuated by a scream, which adds extra power to the dark ritual. As far as I’m concerned, a few additional tracks could have been included here, but this extended “Ajna: Transmissions” remains a pleasant listen nonetheless. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Anja: Transmissions”: Ajna: Transmissions by Grimoire De Occulte About Grimoire De Occulte Grimoire De Occulte is a German duo formed by Bernd Hermanns, also known as “Baal” and the owner of Dunkelheit Produktionen, together with “Philosoph”. The project’s discography traces back to the 2011 cassette EP “Funeral Lands” on Dunkelheit Produktionen, followed by the self-released 2012 rehearsal tape “Rehearsal November 2012″ and the 2017 split 7” “Dschinn… / Atardecer De Mayo” with Mirthless, also on Dunkelheit Produktionen. Further releases include “Ritual Before Thy Fullmoon (Rehearsal)” (2017) and the self-released cassette “Calling The Ancient Fears” (2021), before the duo returned to Dunkelheit Produktionen for the CD album “Sinister Rituals” (2023) and now “Ajna: Transmissions”, issued digitally in 2025 and on CD in 2026.

items.body: Adrian Utley, the guitarist and co-founder of Portishead, has reworked “Étude Op. 25 No. 12” from Polish composer Mariusz Szypura’s “Chopin Residue,” a project that removes the piano entirely from nine of Frédéric Chopin’s best-known piano pieces. The rework arrives today as the latest single from the double album, which Cleopatra Records brings to CD and double vinyl on 16 October; an immersive Blu-ray edition mixed in Dolby Atmos is already available. Chopin Residue by Mariusz Szypura Szypura said working with Utley was a long-held ambition: “Adrian and Portishead are among my favourite musicians. The sound, the approach to making music, the search for unobvious and lo-fi textures, all of it had an enormous influence on me.” Szypura kept the harmonic structure and phrasing of Chopin’s originals while stripping out the instrument itself. He described the decision as a matter of respect rather than provocation: “I rejected the piano immediately. […] I decided Chopin didn’t deserve such profanation. I could only approach this material through the prism of my own sensitivity, harmony, and deconstruction. So I took the piano out. […] The piano was the delivery system, not the content.” Adrian Utley’s rework of ‘Étude Op. 25 No. 12’ “Chopin Residue” splits into two discs: “Deconstructions,” on which Szypura rebuilds nine Chopin pieces with a cast including Lee Ranaldo (Sonic Youth), David Pajo (Slint), Joey Waronker, Gail Ann Dorsey, John McEntire (Tortoise) and John Stanier (Battles), and “Reworks,” on which a second group of artists takes those deconstructed recordings further from the source. Utley’s “Étude Op. 25 No. 12” opens the second disc alongside reworks by Fennesz, Matthew Herbert, Masayoshi Fujita, Sean O’Hagan, Jim O’Rourke, Christine Ott, Benoît Pioulard and Abul Mogard. Szypura described the difference between the two discs directly: “‘Étude Op. 25 No. 12’ is Adrian’s reconstruction, not my piece with his guitar on top. That is the principle of the whole second disc: nine artists, nine rebuilds, each in their own language.” The two discs are designed to be played together as well as separately, an idea that extends into the Blu-ray edition’s Dolby Atmos mix. Szypura said: “They were built to overlap. […] In stereo you hear an arrangement. In Atmos you’re inside the harmonic space with the piano missing from the middle of it. […] That’s not a format upgrade, it’s closer to what the piece was always trying to do.” “Chopin Residue” gets its UK stage premiere at London’s Cadogan Hall on 26 September, as part of the Polish Jazz Festival. Its packaging has also picked up a Bronze A’ Design Award and a Red Dot Award. About Adrian Utley and Mariusz Szypura Adrian Utley was born in Northampton in 1957 and moved to Bristol in the mid-1980s, where he played guitar in touring bands led by jazz organist Big John Patton and drummer Art Blakey’s Jazz Messengers. He co-founded Portishead in Bristol in 1991 with Geoff Barrow and Beth Gibbons, co-producing and playing on the band’s albums “Dummy” (1994), “Portishead” (1997) and “Third” (2008). Outside the band, Utley has recorded and toured with Marianne Faithfull, Jeff Beck and Will Gregory of Goldfrapp, leads his own ensemble Adrian Utley’s Guitar Orchestra, and has scored film and audio work with director Nic Roeg, naturalist David Attenborough and Britain’s National Trust. Mariusz Szypura is a composer, producer and visual artist born in 1972 and based in Warsaw. He started out in the early 1990s in the Poznań rock band Happy Pills before founding his main recording project, Silver Rocket, releasing five albums including “Infinity Fidelity,” a Dolby Atmos record that won Gold for Music/Film Cover at the 2025 European Design Awards. His installation work includes “in:human” at the Centre for Contemporary Art Ujazdowski Castle in Warsaw (2024) and “êkhos” at Lincoln Center during Unsound Festival New York (2024). “Chopin Residue” grew out of that installation practice: Szypura first released the album digitally and on 2LP, 2CD, 2MC and Blu-ray through his own Black Element Label in Warsaw on 28 November 2025, alongside gallery and listening events in New York, Osaka, Los Angeles and Warsaw. Cleopatra Records now extends that release internationally, bringing “Chopin Residue” to CD and double vinyl on 16 October 2026 while the Blu-ray Immersive Edition remains available from its earlier release.

items.excerpt: Sandie Trash announces the single “Poupée Panik,” featuring Eric Debris (Métal Urbain) and Richard Belgium (MI6), the first track revealed from the upcoming album “Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka.” The French post-punk and new wave project has not confirmed a release date for the album itself, and “Poupée Panik” is not yet available on Sandie Trash’s Bandcamp page, Instagram or Facebook. Sandie Trash builds ‘Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka’
items.body: Sandie Trash announces the single “Poupée Panik,” featuring Eric Debris (Métal Urbain) and Richard Belgium (MI6), the first track revealed from the upcoming album “Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka.” The French post-punk and new wave project has not confirmed a release date for the album itself, and “Poupée Panik” is not yet available on Sandie Trash’s Bandcamp page, Instagram or Facebook. Sandie Trash builds ‘Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka’ around the Motel Dakota The nine-track album is set around a recurring fictional location, Room 17 of the Motel Dakota, with several tracks written as character pieces tied to that setting: “La perversita,” “Poupée Panik,” “Élégance déplacée,” “Gloria Dakota” and “Sophie qui aime les avions.” Sandie Trash describes the record as a “sabotage” of eighties nostalgia rather than a nostalgic homage to the decade. Alongside Eric Debris and Richard Belgium, the album credits a wide cast of guest contributors: Emmanuelle 5 (Dead Sexy), Olivier de Joie (Les Fils de Joie), Max Freeth (Ausgang), Karbokroma, Kelsey Warren (Blak Emoji), Jérôme Lefdup (Lefdup & Lefdup), Gilles Le Guen (Denner) and Oli Le Baron (Ici Paris). One track, “I Trash You Fuck Off,” is credited with a guest vocal from Helno, the former Lucrate Milk member who went on to front Les Négresses Vertes until his death in January 1993. Sandie Trash’s announcement does not explain how that vocal appears on a track dated 2026, whether as a sample, an archival recording or another arrangement, and no further detail was available to confirm it. Eric Debris also mixed and mastered the album at ATX Mastering studio. The cover art is by Italian illustrator Volt.B. About Sandie Trash Sandie Trash is a French punk and electro project based in Périgueux, fronted by the singer of the same name and built, album after album, around a rotating cast of guest musicians on individual tracks. The approach dates back at least to 2018, when the project’s “Le French Peep Show” paired a new musician with each song on the record. On Bandcamp, Sandie Trash’s confirmed discography includes the album “Outrageous brune,” released 25 February 2010 through Indies.Music.Productions with vocals from Sandie Trash and Maudd and mixing and mastering by Emmanuel Borie, and the 14-track compilation “Rose chewing-gun & Machine-gum (2006-2017),” released 29 May 2025 and gathering tracks and features from that decade, including contributions from Kloot Per W, Romeo Praly, Kim Ohio Fuzz, Marcel Vanthilt and Nina Courson. “Poupée Panik” and the album built around it, “Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka,” continue that same collaborative format on a larger scale, bringing in musicians tied to Métal Urbain, MI6, Ausgang, Denner and other underground post-punk and EBM circles for a post-punk and new wave record set inside the fictional Motel Dakota.

items.body: These two releases from Anna Fedorova and András Schiff both feature Brahms’ late Opp. 117–119 sets, but Schiff’s also includes Opp. 76 and 116. The most interesting distinction, though, is the choice of instrument: Schiff plays a Blüthner built around 1859. Amazon Presto Apple Amazon Presto Apple Fedorova’s Op. 117 is best defined by her exquisite voice leading, present in each of the three works. In faithfully maintaining the integrity and continuity of the thematic material, she creates a fluid and expansive quality despite the structural minimalism. The melodiousness also elicits different but equally comforting emotions throughout: empathy in the Andante moderato (track 1), gentle yearning in the Andante non troppo (track 2), and gravity in the Andante con moto (track 3). Schiff’s performance is equally effective but in a different manner: the period instrument, while resonant, has a lighter profile than Fedorova’s. This evokes a Classical elegance that we don’t always associate with late Brahms. His Andante moderato from Op. 117 (Disc 2, track 1) expresses a more coy tenderness. The Andante non troppo (Disc 2, track 2) has an even greater degree of fragility and transparency than Fedorova’s. The final piece sounds more subdued and solemn, although the beautiful shimmer of the middle section is not to be overlooked. Op. 118 introduces more distinct personalities throughout, all of which Fedorova faithfully captures. The opening Intermezzo (track 4) may not be as bold or rhapsodic as the reading from Francesco Piemontesi that I reviewed recently, but it is meaningful and contemplative. The A major Intermezzo (track 5) is exquisite, considerably more intimate than I’ve heard elsewhere, and tells of her impressive palette of softer dynamics. The G minor Ballade has a satisfying austerity, which she draws from the full bass register of the piano. The final Intermezzo (track 9) stands out as it convincingly juxtaposes two divergent personalities: a quietness characterized by enigmatic undertones and a drama bolstered by the undulating accompanimental material. Schiff’s Op. 118 opens with a grand, emphatic reading of the first Intermezzo (Disc 2, track 4) that also underscores Brahms’ colorful chromatic complexity. The A major (Disc 2, track 5) is less introverted but instead takes on a brisker tempo that reveals a grazioso profile. I expected his G minor Ballade to move a little faster than Fedorova’s, but it feels even more deliberate and measured; the major middle section, while largely calm, possesses an intriguing undercurrent of suspense thanks to the Blüthner’s lower register, which growls ever so subtly. The F minor Intermezzo (Disc 2, track 7) again carries a Classical undertone that feels almost Schubertian in its refined approach. With the exception of the heroic finale, Op. 119 contains some of Brahms’ most introspective writing. While Fedorova’s B minor Intermezzo (track 10) brings this out, I found the E minor (track 11) surprisingly vibrant and highly responsive to harmonic twists and turns. The C major is quite placid—perhaps too much so; it might benefit from more perkiness and forward movement, as we hear in Richard Goode’s recording. Fedorova’s E-flat Rhapsody, though, proves a most satisfying end to an excellent set: it is full of authority and reminds us of the composer’s signature symphonic profile. If only the recorded dynamics didn’t sound as though they were reaching their limits. In the louder passages here and elsewhere, there is a slight distortion that can be picked up even at low volume. András Schiff (left, photo © Nadia F. Romanini) and Anna Fedorova. Schiff brings out the intricate details of Brahms’ compositional style in his Op. 119. The E minor Intermezzo (Disc 2, track 11) gets off to a slow start, but a patient listen reveals how the pianist makes pointed distinctions between staccato and legato interchanges. His C major Intermezzo flows a bit better than Fedorova’s and gives off a uniquely ballet-like feel. The finale, too, possesses a distinct personality: Schiff purposefully rests on certain beats, creating a particular “gait” that helps emphasize the work’s substantiality. Nearly 15 years separate Op. 76 and Op. 116, and Schiff’s performances reveal the differences between the two. Op. 76 essentially marks the start of Brahms’ late period, but the pianist introduces a more restless, youthful energy, especially in the active passages. The pieces are more loosely connected given their eclectic characters, and he spotlights this individuality in the stark differences between the timidly playful B minor Capriccio (Disc 1, track 3) and its C-sharp minor counterpart (Disc 1, track 6), which is much more stubborn and off-kilter. Op. 116, compositionally more unified, is where we hear Schiff at his most powerful, rousing, and authoritative. The stormy D minor Capriccio (Disc 1, track 16) or the fierce final moments of the last work are perfect examples. Although Schiff offers a slightly wider scope of offerings, both performances are equally compelling and enjoyable—yet undeniably distinct to each musician. Fedorova’s readings evoke the depth and spirituality of Brahms’ late period, while Schiff’s puts an interesting Classical spin on certain works without losing their introspective essence. Recommended Comparisons Brahms: Klavierstücke, Opp. 117-119 Radu Lupu | Wilhelm Kempff | Hélène Grimaud | Paul Lewis Brahms: Klavierstücke, Opp. 76 & 116 Richard Goode | Julius Katchen | Jonathan Plowright | Garrick Ohlsson The form can be filled in the actual website url. items.body: Mental wormholes in the night Strange ideas give a familiar fright Some phantom power pulling you back And onto a completely different track Jack Duckworth has spent years making Soft Riot records that seem to know exactly how ridiculous modern life is, then politely invite the machines responsible over for dinner. On his latest LP, Crux, out now through Possession Records and Minimalkombinat, that dinner appears to have taken a turn. Somebody has started transmitting instructions through the walls, and Duckworth is sitting there with a synthesizer trying to determine whether the voice belongs to inspiration, paranoia, technology, or some unseen bastard who has been rewriting his lines while he sleeps. Ghostwriter sets the idea in motion with a Motorik beat, clipped electronics, and Duckworth’s sprechstimme delivered with the disciplinary authority of someone reading factory regulations during an evacuation. There is something of Nitzer Ebb and Suicide in the chant, Fad Gadget in the nervous intelligence, and Skinny Puppy in the sense that electronic equipment might eventually develop opinions about its owner. Elsewhere, the stylish severity of Japan, Bill Nelson’s eccentric futurism, Simple Minds before stadiums swallowed them, and late-period Wire all seem to inhabit the same crooked apartment building. Prince lurks somewhere downstairs, idly wondering why everybody is dressed so seriously. The song concerns creation becoming possession. Ideas appear without explanation, strange mental tunnels open after dark, and ordinary thought gets interrupted by transmissions whose sender remains unknown. Duckworth turns writer’s intuition into supernatural interference: inspiration as somebody else grabbing the steering wheel. His video makes that concept gloriously physical. Forget the standard musician-stares-meaningfully-at-camera routine. Duckworth does that, but becomes part of a universe of printed graphics, hand animation, projected textures, surreal juxtapositions, and visual jokes that recall Dada photomontage, Saul Bass title sequences, and the wonderfully deranged graphic vocabulary of 80s television. Everything looks cut, pasted, shoved sideways, photographed again, and allowed to misbehave. All animations were made physically, with printed graphics manipulated by hand, while projector imagery was filmed again to produce the backgrounds and textures. Duckworth handled the graphics and editing, with assistance from Leyre Mann Vadillo. That analogue process becomes part of the argument: “This allowed me not only to get off the computer for most of the creation of this video, but also opened up the doors really wide for collaboration with other people in a far more intuitive and inclusive way,” says Duckworth. “This allowed the usage of computer software to be basic and minimal, mainly keying out backgrounds, levels, colourising and layering of the animated footage. As I feel the world of what I recognize as an underground music scene and community keeps getting more absorbed into the world of statistics, data and marketing that is more in line with late-stage capitalism, it was important for me to focus on things in the real world like working with other people, meeting new ones, connecting with people, traveling and performing live. The digital world today is planned, created, and orchestrated by the corporations that build it — a far cry from the more utopian possibilities the internet held when I first got acquainted with it in the 90s. The physical world, however, is something that we still don’t know the purpose of yet, despite thousands of years of humans trying to speculate why it exists. Ultimately, the digital world we’ve created can’t exist without the physical world it sits in — not the other way around.” Watch the video for Ghostwriter below: With Ghostwriter Jack Duckworth has made a song about invisible influence while creating its visual counterpart with scissors, paper, projectors, hands, and other people. In an era increasingly obsessed with converting creativity into metrics, his forthcoming album Crux finds Soft Riot asking a useful question: when an idea suddenly appears inside your head, who exactly handed it to you? Listen to Ghostwriter below and order Crux here. items.body: Where’s the joy in this all? Where’s the light in the dark My hands hide my tears, I feel so lost This first day of Fall There is something especially lonely about being miserable on a day for which everyone else has already chosen your mood. A birthday comes with instructions: answer the messages, accept the affection, make a wish. For Los Angeles post-punk duo DECEITS, The First Day of Fall opens up the awful distance between that public celebration and a private wish to disappear. The calendar, as ever, has failed to consult the person concerned. Following our premiere of the single, the song returns with a video directed by Shutter Visual, whose credits include work with Twin Tribes and Blood Club. Its tightly framed performance brings the song’s distress into uncomfortable proximity, with vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Kevin Moreno and drummer Francisco Saenz caught inside a room that seems to grow smaller as the performance intensifies. Moreno wrote the song on a despondent morning the day before his birthday. Faced with an occasion supposedly reserved for happiness, he found himself confronting the desire not to exist at all. That unhappy collision gives the lyrics their particular ache: another year becomes something to account for, while the prospect of celebration makes an already difficult feeling harder to explain. Autumn provides an apt setting for such thoughts, its gradual retreat from summer matching the impulse to withdraw from everyone wishing you well. The arrangement gives those thoughts a restless physical form. A commanding bassline and forceful drums drive through the song, while reverberant guitars spread outward over gothic synthesizers. There is punk urgency in the rhythm section and a wounded romanticism in the melody, each pulling at the other. Moreno’s singing follows the same uneasy course, moving from a softer, intimate register into high, strained cries as the music gathers force. The spacious production leaves room around his voice without taking any pressure off it. Shutter Visual builds the clip around that pressure. Blue-green light washes across the musicians, with hanging guitars, amplifiers, and the white grid beneath their feet giving the performance space a stark, enclosed character. Close-ups of picking hands and struck cymbals keep returning us to the effort involved in playing, while wider shots catch Moreno bending over his guitar and throwing his head back. Saenz’s drumming supplies a firm center as the camera moves between the two. Elsewhere, Moreno faces the lens with dark makeup trailing beneath his eyes, his pale shirt and decorative collar giving way to black stage clothes in other shots. He grips the microphone, raises his hands to his face, and sings with an increasingly exposed intensity. Blurred movement, doubled faces, and fractured views interrupt the more straightforward performance footage, making his expressions difficult to hold in focus. The visual instability suits a song about feeling estranged from the very life everyone else is congratulating you on having. Near the end, the camera settles on white roses and scattered petals across the gridded floor. Against the room’s severe geometry, the flowers look painfully vulnerable, their associations with affection and celebration left in disarray. It is a fitting image for the song’s birthday premise, and Shutter Visual lets the performance carry the desperation that drove Moreno to write it. The most affecting moments come when his gestures seem to outrun his composure, giving visible shape to what the lyrics struggle to contain. Watch the video for The First Day of Fall below: Since forming in Los Angeles in 2021, Moreno and Saenz have channeled their shared love of the Spanish-language music of their upbringing into a particularly expressive strain of post-punk. Its rhythms, romantic feeling, and emotional directness inform a sound that gives gothic reserve very little room to get comfortable. The First Day of Fall draws on that openness, bringing a difficult private experience into a form that other people can recognize and share. The First Day of Fall is out now, with the demo version also included on the Bandcamp release. Listen below and order the single here. The First Day Of Fall by DECEITS DECEITS continue their Hurt As Much As Me Tour through the United States, followed by an appearance at BLOODFLOWERS — Japan Goth & Post Punk Festival in Tokyo and dates in New Zealand and Australia. Get tickets here. items.body: Fawning, we’re brighter, we’re cautious, Falling like fighters, we’re caustic. Cracked up like actors, we’re lying. Daydreams and nightmares. Sharing cigarettes and leather trousers can feel like a promising start to eternity, until eternity begins to resemble an argument neither person can leave. Berlin’s Night Nail take that unhappy prospect to the dance floor on Vile Train, a gothic rock seduction in which two lovers become so absorbed in each other that escape begins to seem as impossible as happiness. The attraction is considerable; so is the damage. The song previews Infinite Fountain, Night Nail’s fourth studio album, due November 6, 2026, through Icy Cold Records. Its accompanying video reunites the band with director and editor Jean De Oliviera, whose previous collaborations include Hollow Day, Little Armenia, and Narcoleptic Dream Catcher. Vile Train begins with a noise suspended somewhere between a buzz and a screech, while cold guitar tones gather around it with considerable menace. The drums establish their footing before a heavier, sustained riff saws through the opening, its melody making the abrasion strangely inviting. Around the thirty-second mark, the bass enters with a deep, brooding groove, and the guitar shifts into a lower, more resonant register. That change gives the song a mournful richness, setting the scene for Brandon Robert’s dark, swaggering delivery. Repeating synth figures tighten the tension beneath his voice, and roughly a minute in, the chorus sends the arrangement into a more urgent gothic dance beat. The construction is remarkably assured: each entrance increases the pressure, while the bass keeps enough melodic independence to make the groove feel alive. By the three-minute mark, its intricate phrasing has become a hook in its own right, moving beneath Robert’s breathy repetition of “Daydreams and nightmares” as a feminine voice echoes the words in whispers. The song’s pleasure comes from those relationships between the instruments, the way an ominous opening develops into something so physically persuasive. Robert found the initial inspiration during a visit to Pompeii, where a fresco depicting an angel and a demon in an embrace suggested a romance with a particularly poor prognosis. In the song’s conception, two dreamers inhabit separate modern realities until their fantasies bring them together. They exchange clothes, cigarettes, and intimacies, gradually making a prison of the connection that first seemed to offer freedom. Robert describes the result as “dark and brutal truths about love sung in a twisted but beautiful way.” The lyrics give that deterioration a nasty intimacy. Caution sits beside fawning, attraction beside aggression, and the lovers seem increasingly aware of the roles they have been playing. “Some days I wish I was her” carries the confusion further, towards the point where wanting another person begins to erase the distinction between their identity and your own. Against the recurring admission of lies, the fantasy of America offers another possible elsewhere. Every imagined exit seems to lead back to the same two people. Vile Train was mixed and post-produced by William Faith at 13 Studio in Chicago, with co-production by Night Nail in Berlin and additional vocals and guitar from VV & the Void. That combination serves a song whose writing and arrangement make its gothic excess feel earned, with a chorus capable of turning private misery into a crowded dance floor. Directed and edited by Jean De Oliviera, the video gives Vile Train a stark black-and-white treatment, cutting between Robert and bassist Ilija Gavrilenko performing among amplifiers and outdoor shots framed by stone arches and fountain basins. Black leather, dark glasses, and severe makeup give the pair a suitably funereal glamour, while tight shots of fingers on strings bring the song’s instrumental interplay into focus. Robert’s face repeatedly fills the frame, his dark lipstick and pale features isolated against the black background. Grain, scratches, and superimposed silhouettes of reaching hands disturb that severe simplicity, spreading across faces and instruments until the musicians seem caught behind the image itself. Robert’s own gestures towards the lens make the camera feel uncomfortably close, turning performance into something between an invitation and an accusation. The recurring close-ups and grasping hands give the song’s obsession a physical form, suggesting an intimacy that has become impossible to escape. It is an effective visual rendering of what the band calls the “afterlife of relationship hell,” where the desire to hold someone close has acquired a distinctly claustrophobic meaning. Watch the video for Vile Train below: Formed in Los Angeles in 2013, Night Nail relocated to Berlin in 2018, the year their debut album LA Demons appeared on Cleopatra Records. March To Autumn followed through Cold Transmission in 2020, with Fates Explained arriving on Metropolis Records in 2023. The archival release Early Demons and Demos and remix album Fates Remade followed in 2024. Their earlier work with producer Pete Burns of Kill Shelter helped establish a catalogue that connects darkwave electronics with gothic rock’s appetite for emotional extremes. Infinite Fountain also includes mixing and post-production work by Sven Wolff of Patenbrigade: Wolff. Night Nail plans to support the album with shows across the US, UK, and Europe during 2026–2027. In the meantime, explore their back catalog on Bandcamp. items.album: Faded Pulse Finds Solace in the Past on Ethereal Goth Album “Elysia”
items.excerpt: Hear a voice call through the trees Leave this dying world behind Come along and follow me To the meadows of our minds A good fairy tale knows that beauty can get you into trouble, and that an invitation to dance may come with terms and conditions nobody bothered to explain.
