items.body: Hear a voice call through the trees Leave this dying world behind Come along and follow me To the meadows of our minds A good fairy tale knows that beauty can get you into trouble, and that an invitation to dance may come with terms and conditions nobody bothered to explain. For Washington, D.C.’s Faeryn Johnson, the musician behind Faded Pulse, that uneasy invitation opens onto Elysia, a second album where ethereal wave, goth, folk, and dream pop meet the romantic imagination of medieval poetry and Victorian painting. Acoustic guitars, hammered dulcimer, electric bass, and ambient synthesizers accompany water spirits, waiting maidens, and woodland gatherings whose hosts have questionable intentions. The route here runs through the synthpop of 2025’s Submission and the more ethereal leanings of that year’s Fallen EP, with a decisive turn taken while watching Monica Richards perform with Strange Boutique in Washington. Johnson’s affection for the 1990s Projekt catalogue supplies another set of coordinates: Lycia, Love Spirals Downwards, Black Tape for a Blue Girl, and Unto Ashes sit alongside the folk of Pentangle and Donovan. There is a generous curiosity at work, the kind that can find room for both a Slowdive bassline and a William Morris poem without making either feel like an unlikely guest. Johnson’s background in art history gives Elysia a visual life as rich as its musical references. Waterhouse’s paintings, the Arts and Crafts movement, and Art Nouveau belong to the same imaginative world as thrifted velvet, medieval dress, and an old copy of Tennyson found in an antique shop. Beneath the finery lie practical questions about courage, community, and how to remain attentive to the living world. This gathering of fairies may be perilous, but the hope is that listeners return from it with a renewed appetite for their own lives. We spoke with Johnson about the records that opened those doors, the literature and paintings behind Elysia, and the enduring possibilities of ethereal music, from a hammered dulcimer to a dream performance among the art and architecture of the Cloisters. Before Faded Pulse, what first opened the door to the Gothic imagination for you? Was there a particular record, book, painting, or encounter that made you feel you had found somewhere you belonged? Faded Pulse: I started getting into the gothic scene when I was around 14 years old, and at that time my most essential record was The Cure’s Pornography. I loved the dense, almost psychedelic sound of the album. I’ve probably overplayed that record way too much at that age. Yet it really cemented my love for atmosphere and dense sound design. Robert Smith’s honest and vulnerable lyricism made me feel so seen and got me through so much. Between Submission, Fallen, and Elysia, your music has moved further into folk and ethereal wave. What was happening in your life and listening habits that encouraged that change, and what could you express through these arrangements that you hadn’t explored before? Faded Pulse: When I first started “Submission” around 2022, I was very much into the New Wave and Synthpop sounds of the 80s, and that really shows on that album, although my listening has always been more eclectic. One big influence on Elysia was psych and folk of the 60s and 70s, particularly bands like Pentangle; their album Solomon’s Seal was super influential on me, especially songs like “Willy O’Winsbury”. Donovan was another big influence; you can really hear it on songs like “Will Thy Heart Be True,” where I go for a more folky, ballad-type song. I have always had a huge love for the 90’s ethereal scene. The moment I knew I wanted to move sonically towards that was when I saw Strange Boutique live at the Black Cat in D.C. in 2025. Seeing Monica Richards on stage and hearing the music live was really a light-bulb moment for me. Ethereal allows me to experiment more with unusual instrumentation and also lets the music take people to another world. Although I enjoyed making synth pop, here I can play with classical, folk, ambient, and even more rock-oriented structures. It’s so much more playful and freeing. I feel like Faded Pulse would have been a perfect fit for Projekt Festival, especially the 1997 edition. How were you first introduced to the label and its artists, and was there a particular band or record that sparked your affinity for that strain of ethereal music? Faded Pulse: Projekt has a special place in my heart and is probably one of my favorite labels ever. My essential four artists from the record label are Black Tape, Lycia, Love Spirals, and Unto Ashes. Black Tape for a Blue Girl’s “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” is one of my all-time favs; it is a masterpiece in its own right in sound design and atmosphere, and it’s both deeply haunting and romantic. I feel like Love Spirals Downwards Idylls is glaringly obvious as one of the influences on Elysia, and I feel it is their most essential record. It’s hard for me to choose a Lycia album because they’re my favorite band on the label, but if I had to choose, it would be “A Day in the Stark Corner”. It’s equal parts dreamy, cold, and bleak. Unto Ashes serves everything I look for in a band: medieval instruments and sounds, folk and darkwave synths. I feel like their album “Empty into white” is so sonically rich and put together, sinister yet dreamy. I’m not sure how I even stumbled on the label, which feels fitting, like it came to me almost in a dream; it is the most influential group of artists for me. There’s something about Elysia that feels entirely at home in the pages of Propaganda or Carpe Noctem. What feels special to you about the Gothic culture of the ’90s, and how have you encountered that period through its music, magazines, photography, and fashion? Faded Pulse: Funnily enough, I own an issue of Propaganda, No. 22, and I wanna say it’s from 1994-1996. I have very fond memories of reading Propaganda magazines in high school on the Internet Archive. I am a historian at heart and love to learn everything I can about culture, music, and fashions of any time period I study. The 90’s, to me, feel somehow criminally underrated, even though it was when the gothic scene was at its peak and fully found itself and diversified into many different interests. I feel the worship of the 80s has caused people to overlook how creative the scene was in the 90s. Even now, somehow darkwave from the 90s is still more experimental and fresh than the very 80s-oriented sounds we get today. As for the fashion, I would study a lot of the pictures on Pinterest from magazines, club shoots, or people’s personal uploads, and when I went thrifting, I would look for similar items. PVC, Satins, Silks, and Velvet are all mainstays in my closet thanks to the 90s, haha. “Meadow of My Mind” and “Upon the Heavens” feel like a bridge between Cocteau Twins and the more romantic corners of the Projekt catalogue. How do you approach the relationship between voice and guitar in these songs, especially when both seem capable of carrying the melody or dissolving into one another? Faded Pulse: Much like the bands before me, I kind of treat the voice as just another instrument. When recording a lot of these songs, I wanted the guitar and voice to mesh well. In meadow of my mind, the voice and guitar switch throughout the song, giving them space to drive the song along without clashing. In “Meadow of My Mind,” you sing, “Leave this dying world behind,” yet you’ve described Elysia as something beyond escapism. What does that inner refuge make possible for you, and what do you hope listeners bring back from it into their everyday lives? Faded Pulse: To me, “Meadow of my Mind” is about the love of nature, to put it plainly. When listeners “Leave the realm of Elysia,” I want people to bring that sort of magic into their everyday lives. Whether that be getting involved in their local communities, making art, or reading poetry. Whatever it is that makes you feel connected to the world around you. “Upon the Heavens” uses the language of prayer, reaching toward a divine presence and asking to be heard and healed. What is your relationship with that devotional language, and how did you arrive at the kind of sacred experience you wanted the song to convey? Faded Pulse: To me, music is very spiritual, and I definitely wanted Upon the Heavens to emulate that in some way. It’s not a song devoted to a particular deity or religion, but it is about reaching out and feeling something greater. I feel this all the time through music, when I listen to a song that just makes me float away or feel high on euphoria. I mean, historically speaking, music is how people connect to the otherworld and is used in ritual, even though it is now far removed from its sacred roots. Music still feels deeply spiritual and otherworldly, and I think that’s truly what the song conveys. “Lamia’s Kiss” brings to mind Dead Can Dance’s exploration of musical traditions beyond rock, with an experimental quality that feels ancient and unfamiliar at once. Which specific traditions, recordings, or instruments informed it, and how did you develop its musical character? Faded Pulse: The sounds of the Middle East and the Mediterranean very much inspire Lamia’s kiss. A lot of the bands I liked, like Lovespirals, DCD, and Rajna, had eastern influence in their music, so it kinda bled into my consciousness. Rather than writing cliched lyrics about her as a figure, I wanted the song to emulate what it would feel like to be caught in her hypnotic gaze, to be pulled in. Instrumentally, I wanted the Dulcimer to be the lead on the song, which I feel really harnesses that archaic, almost ancient vibe that I wanted the song to have. I also grew up in Asia for a short time. I do think it had a musical effect on me, and it seems only natural that an experience like that would creep into my music in some way. What first drew you to Lamia as a figure? Did you come to her through mythology, Keats’s poem, a painting, or another interpretation, and what interests you about the meeting of beauty, desire, and danger in her story? Faded Pulse: It’s a little bit of all of that. Keats’s poem is definitely an inspo, as is Waterhouse’s iconic painting. I am also a Lilith and Hecate Devotee; the lamia is associated with both, so it’s almost devotional. I also love serpentine imagery and symbolism, as well as the figure of the femme fatale, so it is essentially a collage of many different ideas and feelings. “Fair Lady in Gold” has a baroque richness and a medieval atmosphere, particularly in the bright, struck-string sound that suggests a hammered dulcimer. How did you build that arrangement, and who—or what—is the lady at its center? Faded Pulse: For “Fair Lady in Gold,” I knew I wanted to have a few instrumental tracks on the album. The main instruments here are my Dusty Strings hammered dulcimer and my Korg Minilogue for ambient synths. There is no single song as an influence; rather, months and weeks of studying and listening to music from the Renaissance and medieval period that shaped this song. When I first started writing “The Lady in Gold,” I was envisioning Cordelia from King Lear in a painting by Edwin Austin Abbey. Although her gown is yellow, it is not even close to gold, haha. However, a woman with a golden pooling Bliaut gown was what I was envisioning when creating the song, so the name kinda stuck. “Summerland” seems to occupy a meeting place between Dead Can Dance and Cocteau Twins, while its lyrics describe being drawn into a fairy gathering. How welcoming did you want that invitation to feel, and how much uncertainty or danger belongs within its beauty? Faded Pulse: Summerland is definitely a song where I wanted the listener to be taken away by the fae, where it’s both exhilarating and panic-inducing. To be led away and dancing with beings who look human, yet there is something quite off about them, and strange things happen around them. I wanted to evoke the same feelings I had reading Irish fairy tales, where the stories of the fae are both wondrous and terrifying in equal measure. I think it’s a great metaphor for nature itself. Beautiful yet dangerous. “Undine” recalls the dreamier side of 4AD, alongside Faith and the Muse and Lycia, but its bassline and guitar flourishes also make ethereal wave’s goth and post-punk origins audible. How conscious are you of that connection when writing, and what does the bass allow you to do beneath such expansive arrangements? Faded Pulse: The bassline for Undine was heavily inspired by the bassline in Slowdive’s “Ballad of Sister Sue.” I knew I wanted this waltzy song where the bass carried much of the song’s sway. To me, the bass here is the most important; it just wouldn’t sound the same with a synth bass. It really gives the song that romantic rhythm I feel it needed. The words to “Undine” address the water-born figure directly, questioning her lover’s constancy and encouraging her to voice her feelings. Whose voice did you imagine addressing her, and what did you want your interpretation to reveal about her beyond the familiar tragedy? Faded Pulse: With Undine, I knew I really wanted to do a melancholic song about a siren, where the song itself is almost like a lament, where it feels like a spell is being cast onto the listener. The voice that carries the song is part third-person narrator and part Undine’s voice. The Chorus is nonsensical and is a made-up language, but it is Undine casting her spell, hoping and praying to keep Huldbrand’s love. The third-person voice beckons Undine to own her sadness and heartbreak to sing what’s in her heart and drown in her tears, tragically ending the knight’s life, but also having the strength to embrace her own emotions of love and betrayal. “Will Thy Heart Be True?” has the feel of an ethereal folk ballad, with its knight, waiting maiden, and tests of courage. Which Arthurian or medieval texts informed the song, and what does the question of remaining true mean to you personally? Faded Pulse: I think the concept of knight and maiden came to me through William Morris’s poem “Two Red Roses Across the Moon.” Although I’ve been a fan of Morris for a few years, I first heard of it when I visited the American Arts and Crafts Museum and saw a mural depicting the maiden from the poem waiting for her knight, who was off at war. Although I love the stereotypical depiction of the medieval romance trope, the song really isn’t solely about that. It is about staying strong during dark times and finding the courage to go on, which I feel is extremely relevant. Now, the question “Will Thy Heart be True?” is really asking, “Do you have the strength to keep fighting the good fight?” even when it seems hopeless. Your influences include Romantic literature, medieval poetry, and Victorian fairy tales. Which writers have most shaped your imagination—Keats, Christina Rossetti, William Morris, or perhaps someone less immediately expected? Could you take us through one passage or story that found its way into Elysia? Faded Pulse: One of my biggest influences was Alfred Lord Tennyson’s Idylls of the King, a book I thrifted in an antique shop. It features a poetic retelling of Arthurian legends, and although none of its stories made it into Elysia, I knew I wanted Elysia to evoke the feeling of magic, mystery, and romance that the book gave me. Poems like Coleridge’s Christabel and Keats’s La Belle Dame sans Merci were hugely influential as well. Keats’s story of the Faery woman leading the gullible knight astray was definitely an inspo for Summerland. Your art-history background brings the Pre-Raphaelites, Art Nouveau, and the Arts and Crafts movement into the album’s conception. Is there a particular work by an artist such as Burne-Jones, Waterhouse, or Mucha that you could place beside one of these songs and explain the connection? Faded Pulse: Rather than a single painting, artwork, or artist, Elysia sounds like the movements as a whole and what they were trying to achieve. To me, I want people to look at any art from any of those movements and instantly think of a song from Elysia. But if I had to choose an image to associate with the album, I would choose Waterhouse’s Ophelia, as it was one of the few paintings that made me think, “I want to make music that emulates how this painting feels.” Your photographs feature flowing robes, a circlet, a sword, woodland, and Gothic architecture. Which historical garments, designers, films, or figures inform your sense of dress, and how much of that appearance comes from making or adapting things yourself? Faded Pulse: A lot of Elysia’s costumes are based on a combination of different things. For me, it was studying fashion history throughout the Middle Ages, a lot of the Medieval revival clothing coming out of the goth scene in the 90s, and of course, fantasy films like The Lord of the Rings (Particularly the elves). Photographs of Lisa Hammer and Monica Richards in the 90s and 00s were also influential on me. To me, Lisa is a modern Pre-Raphaelite fashion icon, and I definitely wanted to emulate that for Elysia. A lot of the wardrobe for the photos was thrifted or modified to achieve that vibe. What do you think made ethereal wave such a natural home for medieval romance, folklore, and mystery? Within your own music, what do those older forms of imagination allow you to say about love, longing, or belonging in the present? Faded Pulse: I think there’s something very classic about medieval folklore and stories. They feel very timeless with their usage of romance, bravery, and fighting for something you think is worth fighting for. They capture what it means to be human and to be alive. I think Medieval and Ethereal are so drawn to each other because they both have a sense of whimsy and otherworldliness. I think this element of fantasy is so unique to Ethereal outside of the other core genres of the gothic scene. With ethereal, I can weave stories and ambiance that fully immerse the listener into the world I want to create, and I think that’s why fairytales and ethereal go so well together; it’s a perfect mesh of storytelling and sonic immersion. An enduring part of the Gothic imagination is its embrace of mystery and the wonders of nature. Do you feel that connection is more important than ever in this age of AI, and what role can music play in keeping that sense of wonder alive? Faded Pulse: I think music is more important now than ever in the age of AI. It requires you to engage no matter what, to let go, sit down, and spend your time listening, to feel something. I think music is intrinsically human, and I feel that when people go out to clubs or venues for shows and connect with those around them, it really helps them disconnect from the haze of being online all the time and brings them into the present. There is something magical about watching people perform and bring something out of you. That is something that AI could never replace. If you could present Elysia in a setting entirely of your choosing, what would a Faded Pulse performance look and feel like? How would the space, clothing, and instrumentation help bring listeners into these songs, and what would you want them to feel when they stepped outside again? Faded Pulse: I think two of my dream performance locations would be a medieval ruin or within the Met Cloisters Museum in New York. I feel like being surrounded by actual medieval art and architecture would really set the ambiance. One thing I’ve heard of is that bands in the 90s would have incense burning on stage. I don’t know how true that is, and of course, venues would never allow that now, but I think something like frankincense or sandalwood would be my chosen scent, and I feel like playing with multiple senses would really elevate the performance. For dress, I think it would be cool to have a lot of the new-agey medieval revival looks from the nineties that were popular in the scene, and, of course, I would encourage everyone to participate in dressing up if they so choose. For me, I want the audience to feel like they entered another realm, dreamy and untethered, and when they leave, feeling like they had a spiritual awakening.§ For all its mythic tales of knights, faeries, and enchanted waters, Elysia is an album that keeps returning to the ordinary work of being present: listening closely, making something, finding courage, and spending time with other people. Johnson’s ideal audience might gather in velvet beneath medieval arches, but the invitation extends well beyond that imagined evening. There is room for wonder in a borrowed book, a local show, or an afternoon among the trees, and Faded Pulse offers plenty of reasons to make room for it. Faded Pulse’s Elysia is out now. Listen to the album below and order here. Elysia by Faded Pulse Follow Faded Pulse Instagram Bandcamp The post “Leave This Dying World Behind” — Faded Pulse Finds Solace in the Past on Ethereal Goth Album “Elysia” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Stabbing Westward Wither – ReWired COP International Re-recording a classic album is a risky proposition for any band or artist. Even leaving aside the shady practice of creating soundalike recordings to get in on streaming and sync royalties, the upside of recreating your own work is dubious; technically better performances, recording or production isn’t an improvement when a classic LP’s appeal is in familiarity, shortcomings and all. The best case scenario is that you come up with an interesting alternate take on your own material, but the more common outcome is sounding like a cover band. Thankfully, in the case of Stabbing Westward’s Wither – ReWired, a completely new version of the band’s 1996 breakthrough sophomore album Wither, Blister, Burn + Peel, the band have taken an approach that justifies the endeavor. Signed during the industrial rock’s brief moment of mainstream relevance in the 90s, the original record had catchy songs and benefited hugely from frontman Christopher Hall’s oh-so dramatic alt-rock vocals, but notably buried the majority of the band’s electronic elements beneath mountains of guitar chug. Wither – ReWired addresses that in a way that merely doing a new mix of the original tapes (if that were even an option) couldn’t, by not just recreating, but fully rearranging the songs to give the programming and synthwork equal billing. The results are striking in an A to B comparison of each version. Tracks that felt like lesser moments such as opener “I Don’t Believe” and “Crushing Me” are given a whole new life, the former by wedding a strong programmed rhythm section to the proceedings, the latter by upping the tempo and dialing back the original’s turgid guitars in favour of a sharp, forward moving arrangement. In the case of the record’s best and most memorable moments, such as the rock radio hit “What Do I Have to Do?”, things are left well enough alone, with minor tweaks to programming and the mix to keep it consistent with the rest of the record’s sound. In fact, they stick so close to how you expect those cuts to sound that the small changes stick out; Hall changes some of his vocal phrasing on the chorus to “Shame” in a way that feels wrong at first, but becomes comfortable after a few listens. The other important aspect of Wither – ReWired is in how its songs are sequenced as a listening experience. Where the 1996 original frontloads the record’s singles and most commercial cuts, the new version places songs in an order that feels like it makes more sense. “Slipping Away” is moved from the closing spot, its new club-ready iteration placed to pick things up from the mid-tempo melodrama of “Why?”, replaced by a revamped version of B-side “Agekata (Dawn)” whose more atmospheric synth textures better fit the role. “So Wrong” and “Inside You” (a deep cut that is secretly one of the band’s best moments) have significant time shaved off and are placed to keep the momentum and emotion of the record up leading into the final third. The amount of effort into making a genuinely new, but not unfamiliar album are considerable, and act as evidence that this is anything but a cash-in. Stabbing Westward could have churned out a quick and dirty version of their live set in studio and called it a day, but instead Wither ReWired is a genuinely considered undertaking by a band who understand who they were, who they are, and how to reconcile the thirty year gap in those incarnations. Buy it. Wither – ReWired by Stabbing Westward The post Stabbing Westward, “Wither – ReWired” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: 2026.09.23 デビュー20周年を迎え、ベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタ全5曲に挑む新倉瞳さん。なぜ今、ベートーヴェンなのか？ 7歳でチェロと出会ったきっかけから、音楽家として大切にしていること、憧れの音楽家、新しいジャンルへの挑戦まで……新倉さんの音楽人生と「今」が見えてくる50の質問を前後編でお届けします。 ONTOMO編集部 東京・神楽坂にある音楽之友社を拠点に、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」の企画・取材・編集をしています。「音楽っていいなぁ、を毎日に。」を掲げ、やさしく・ふかく・おもしろ... 詳しく見る デビュー20周年の節目にベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタ全曲に挑む 1. デビュー20周年おめでとうございます！ 20年前の自分に、今の新倉さんから一言かけるとしたら、何と言いますか？ 新倉 「安心していいよ」と言いたいです。自分が思っている自分と、他人から見える自分には、どうしても差があります。100人の人がいたら、100通りの自分の見え方があると思うんです。 20年前は「こうでなければいけない」とすごく気にしていました。でも今は、みんなが思ってくださった自分が自分でしかないと思えるようになりました。自分が思っていることを、意外とちゃんと見てくださっている方々もいらっしゃるので、そういったところでリラックスして、安心して楽しんでいればいいよ、と言いたいですね。 新倉瞳（にいくら・ひとみ） 桐朋学園大学音楽学部を首席で卒業し、皇居桃華楽堂新人演奏会に出演して御前演奏を行う。その後スイスに渡り、バーゼル音楽院ソリストコース・教職課程の両修士課程を最高点で修了。これまでに毛利伯郎、堤剛、トーマス・デメンガ、マーティン・ツェラー（バロック・チェロ）の各氏に師事。国内外で数多くの賞を受賞し、2017年に第18回ホテルオークラ音楽賞、2020年度に第19回齋藤秀雄メモリアル基金賞チェロ部門を受賞。桐朋学園大学在学中にEMI Music Japanより『鳥の歌』でCDデビューし、同レーベルから3枚、アールアンフィニからは『11月の夜想曲～委嘱作品集』を含む4枚のソロアルバムをリリース。ほかにも多数のアルバムを発表している。 かつてカメラータ・チューリッヒのソロ首席チェリストとして活躍し、スイスを拠点にヨーロッパや中央アジア、日本でもソリストや室内楽奏者として幅広く活動する。近年はクレズマー音楽や民族音楽にも造詣を深め、音楽祭に招かれワークショップやレクチャーコンサートも行う。カザフスタンの民俗楽器ドンブラも演奏し、2025年にはカザフスタン国営放送で日本人として異例の紹介を受けた。 使用楽器は宗次コレクションより貸与のマッテオ・ゴフリラー（1710年製）。2026年にデビュー20周年を迎えた。 2. 20周年の節目として、12月3日に俳優の南沢奈央さんの語りとともにベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタを舞台のように届ける演奏会「ベートーヴェンの小径」を開催されます。まず、ベートーヴェンを取り上げようと思った理由を教えてください。どんな演出になるのでしょうか？ 新倉 私はいろんなジャンルの音楽に興味を持って活動してきましたが、20周年ということで、いわゆる「ザ・クラシック」みたいなプログラムに取り組みたいという思いもありました。これまで民俗音楽にも多く取り組んできましたが、ベートーヴェンの作品も紐解いていくと、民俗音楽との関連が見えてきます。だからこそ、節目の年にベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタ全曲を取り上げるのは、すごくいいのではないかと思いました。 さらに、私のデビュー20周年の次の年がベートーヴェンの没後200年なので、長い期間で、お祭りみたいにできるかなと思った次第です。 演出については、当日までのお楽しみです。ただ、音楽をいわゆる舞台の主役にして、チェロ・ソナタが本編となって、語りの部分が幕間をつないでいくような感じにしたいと思っています。 3. 「ベートーヴェンの小径」では、演奏だけでなく構成・脚本・演出も手がけられます。なぜこのような舞台形式でベートーヴェンを届けたいと思われたのでしょうか？ 新倉 ベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタを改めて勉強して、ベートーヴェンの生きてきた背景や彼が残した言葉などいろいろなものをリサーチしていくうちに、ものすごく面白いと思ったんです。そして、演奏で伝えることが使命ではありますが、せっかくだったら物語を交えてみるのはどうかな、と思いました。 南沢奈央さんとは、以前『罪と罰』という舞台でご一緒したことがあって、そのときも音楽が物語に介入していくような演出でした。南沢さんとその後ご飯に行ったときに、彼女も今年がデビュー20周年だと知り、「じゃあ何か一緒にやれたらいいね」と言って別れたんです。 その帰り道に、もし彼女にベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタでご一緒していただけるんだったら、そういった物語を本当に組み込めるかもしれないと思いついて。いろんな点と点が、ピーンとつながったんです。 もうひとつの拠点、スイスで、著名な音楽家の方が演奏曲の背景をさらっとお話ししてからコンサートをするのを見て、すごく勉強になったんです。「こういうひと言があると入っていきやすいな」と。だから、演出とか脚本という言葉にするとすごくドラマティックですが、自然な流れなんじゃないかなと思っています。総合プロデュースとして、作曲家と曲の魅力や、自分が思っていることをお伝えできるきっかけになるんじゃないかなと思っています。 新倉瞳 × 南沢奈央「ベートーヴェンの小径」 4. ベートーヴェンの5曲のチェロ・ソナタの中で、今のご自身に一番近いと感じる作品はどれですか？ 新倉 今の自分に一番近いと感じるのは、もしかしたら3番かもしれません。 私は、そのときに取り組んでいる曲が一番大事だと思うタイプ。でも、ベートーヴェンの5曲のソナタをそれぞれ見ていくと、1番と2番はベートーヴェン自身がピアノを弾いていたこともあって、ピアノが主役で、チェロはオブリガートのような役割なんですね。 それに対して第3番は、ベートーヴェンがいわゆるチェロ・ソナタとして舞台に乗せることを意識して作っているので、第1番、第2番とは全然違うんです。第4番、第5番になると、さらに即興的な要素も入ってきます。 そう考えると、自分が演奏家として人前に出るという意味では、第3番が一つのきっかけのような存在なのかなと思います。ロマンティックな部分もすごくあって、ロマン派への入り口にもなっていますし。 ただ、ベートーヴェン自身がソナタに対していろいろなアプローチをしていったように、私自身も変化していくと思うんです。だから、数年後には「やっぱり第5番かな」と言っているかもしれません。 初めてチェロを弾いたときに「もっといい音を出したい」と思った 5. チェロを始めたきっかけを教えてください。 新倉 もともと母がピアニストで、お腹の中にいるときからピアノを聴いていました。自然ななりゆきで母からピアノを教わっていたんですが、普段は優しい母なのに、ピアノの前では急に角がはえてきて（笑）。それで、だんだんピアノが怖くなってしまいました。 当時、父の仕事の関係でドイツに住んでいたこともあって、音楽がいろんな方とのコミュニケーションのツールになるということは、よく感じていました。音楽自体はもちろん大好きだったけど、ピアノを弾くことが怖くなってしまった私を見かねて、7歳くらいのときに母がドイツのトーンハレというライン川のほとりにある劇場に、よくコンサートに連れて行ってくれました。 母は、ピアノでなくてもハープやフルートといった女性が構えて美しい楽器を趣味でいいから演奏してくれたらといいなと思っていたらしいんです。でも、その頃オーケストラや室内楽を聴いて、「チェロって、すごく支えているのに主役にもなれるし、いろんな面があって、何より音色がきれいで、いい楽器だな」と思って、母に「あれがやりたい」と言ったんです。 そのとき母は、「足を開く楽器を選んだ！」と思ってびっくりしたらしいんですけど、8歳の誕生日にチェロがやってきました。 7歳にしてチェロに魅了されたという新倉さん 6. 初めてチェロを弾いたとき、どんな印象を持ちましたか？ 新倉 もちろん、体に当たって音が響くことには「わー」と感動しました。 でも、まだ小さかったのでフルサイズではなくて1/2サイズの子ども用のチェロだったんです。大人の演奏で聴いていたよりも、「あれ、なんか音があんまりよくない？」と思って。「もっといい音を出したい」と思いました。思っている音色じゃない、というのはすごく覚えています。当時から早くフルサイズになりたいと思っていました。 7. 子どもの頃、一番好きだったチェロの曲は何ですか？ 新倉 今思うと、ヴィヴァルディのチェロ・ソナタ第5番ですね。 わりと小さいときに取り組んだ曲だったんです。ヴィヴァルディの《四季》がすごく好きだったので、「チェロでもヴィヴァルディが弾けるんだ！」というところで、子どもの頃から好きでした。チェロを始めて1、2年後、わりと早い段階で取り組んでいました。 ヴィヴァルディ：チェロ・ソナタ第5番第1楽章 8. 「音楽家になろう」と決めたのは、いつ頃でしたか？ 新倉 中学生のときです。ピアノがちょっと怖くなって以降、チェロに関してはものすごく自由に、練習したいときに練習して、ほかの習い事も並行していました。クラシックバレエ、水泳、テニス、塾など、いろいろさせてもらっていたんです。 中学生のときには、絵描きや美術の道に進むことにも憧れがあって、どちらにしても芸術なんですけれども、少し悩んでいました。そんなときに、パブロ・カザルスの国連でのスピーチで、「わたしの故郷カタルーニャの鳥はピース、ピースと鳴くのです」とおっしゃっているのを聞いて、「どうして人間は争っているんだ」と思ったんです。 それはいまだに消えないテーマなんですけど、「音楽がそういった平和にちゃんと響くことができるんだ」と思って、絶対に音楽家になろうと思いました。 クレズマー音楽との出会いによって「優等生」から解放 9. 音楽家になっていなかったら、何になりたかったですか？ 新倉 絵描きに憧れがありました。薄い色を重ねる水彩画は苦手で、はっきりとした、わりとおどろおどろしい絵を描いていました（笑）。 10. これまでの音楽人生で、ご自身が大きく変わったと感じた出来事は？ 新倉 いまだに真面目気質ではあるんですけれども、今はだいぶ「不真面目になること」に、いい意味で慣れるようになったなと思っています。 大学生のときにデビューして、優等生でいないといけないという時期もありましたが、スイスで東ヨーロッパのクレズマー音楽に出会って、プロもアマチュアもいるバンドに参加するようになったんです。そこで、「優等生である必要ないな」と思って。音楽が好きで集まって、みんなで弾いている気持ちって、すごく大事だなと思うようになりました。 そこからすごく気持ちが落ち着いて、そうすると、キャリアもなぜか追いついてきたというか。クレズマー音楽に出会って、自分が「優等生でいなくちゃいけない」という意識がなくなったときに、すごく解放されたなと思います。 クレズマー音楽も収録したアルバム『魂柱と鞴』 11. もしチェロ以外の楽器をマスターできるとしたら、何を選びますか？ 新倉 実は2つあって、1つは昔から打楽器が大好きなんです。リズムってやっぱりすごいなというイメージがあります。今も趣味でサンバヘギというサンバの太鼓を叩いています。実は音楽之友社さんの前からスタートする神楽坂のパレードで、何回か叩いたことがあります。 あとは歌ですね。自分の声が楽器というのは憧れがあります。それができないから、チェロで歌を表現している部分があるのかなと思います。 歌は自分が楽器だから、それがダイレクトに伝わると思うんです。でも、それって生まれ持ったものもあると思うので、私は次はもっとカラオケでバリバリ歌える声質で生まれてきたいなと思います。 2025年「化け猫フェスティバル」より 編集部員にとっておなじみの会社周辺の光景に新倉さんが打楽器を演奏する姿が……！ 動画は新倉瞳さんのInstagramで！ 大切にしているのは「一音入魂」 12. 新倉さんにとって、チェロの一番好きなところはどこですか？ 新倉 歌を表現できるところです！ 13. 一番の思い出の曲は？ 新倉 エルガーのチェロ協奏曲です。取り組んでいた中学生のときに、祖父が亡くなったんです。私にとって初めての大好きな人の旅立ちだったので、人間の魂というものが音に乗るという経験を初めてしました。叫びきれない思いをチェロに乗せて叫べた、そういった経験ができました。 14. 生涯でチェロ協奏曲を1曲しか弾けないとしたら、どの作品を選びますか？ 新倉 これもエルガーのチェロ協奏曲です。高校受験のときにも取り組みましたが、エルガーはとても深みがあるので、大人になってから取り組むというイメージがあったんですけれど、ドロドロした絵を描くタイプだったからこそ、その深い音楽にシンパシーを感じていたのかもしれません。 新倉さんによるエルガー：チェロ協奏曲 15. 演奏するときに、一番大切にしていることは何ですか？ 新倉 「一音入魂」です。一音一音、そこに何か意味がある音を出したいと思っています。 なんとなく音符を追うのではなく、「作曲家はどうしてこの音を残して、私はどのようにそれを汲み取ったらよいのだろう」とすり合わせて、音に魂を込めたいなと思っています。 16. 練習中など壁にぶつかったときはどうやって乗り越えますか？ 新倉 結局、ひたすら納得いくまで練習するしかないなと思います。私は悩みをそのままにしておけないタイプなので、悩みきることのほうが気持ちいいんです。ぶつかっていきますね。 練習したくない気分のときは、あまり悩まないで、やめて、ご飯を食べに行くなど気分転換して、また向き合います。 本番前のルーティンはなし！ 17. 本番前は緊張するタイプですか？ 新倉 準備が整っていると、あまりしないかな。もうやるしかないと思っているから。逆に、練習中のほうが「これ、間違えたらどうしよう」と緊張することもあります。そういうことを練習中に考えて、本番前は「ここまでやったから、もう大丈夫だろう」と思って挑みます。 18. 本番前に必ずすること、ルーティンはありますか？ 新倉 あまり決めないほうがいいと思っています。日本のコンサートホールのように楽屋がきちんとある環境ばかりではなく、海外の教会で寒い日にいきなり弾かなければならないこともある。そうすると、ルーティンを決めていて、それができなかったときに焦ってしまうんじゃないかなと思うんです。 なので、練習を始めるときは曲をパッと弾いて、弾けなかったところが自分のウィークポイントだと思うようにしています。 19. 「今日はいい演奏ができた」と感じるのは、どんなときですか？ 新倉 結局、自分にはどうしても厳しくなってしまうので、共演者やお客さまがいい顔、いい表情をしていたら「よかったのかな」と思えます。自分基準ではあまり判断できないので、ほかの人がいい顔をしているかどうかで「よかったのかな」と思えます。 ちなみにスタイルキープの秘訣は「服のサイズを変えないこと」だそう！ 20. 今、一番弾いていて楽しい作曲家は誰ですか？ 新倉 今はベートーヴェンです。常に変わっているんですが、今はベートーヴェンに改めて取り組んでいて、新しい発見がたくさんあります。 以前に聴いたときとは、やっぱり自分が変わっている。特にベートーヴェンは、私が幼少期に聴いてきた演奏は、どちらかというとロマンティックな演奏が多かったんです。 ベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタ1番、2番は、チェロがオブリガート的な役目だと先ほどお話ししましたが、それでもチェロがリッチに演奏されることが今まですごく多かった。 でも、今改めて勉強し直してみると、ピアノとチェロの対話が面白いんです。例えば、チェロから始まるフレーズだと思って弾いていた部分が、改めて見るとピアノから呼応する形で出てきているんだな、と。そう考えると、「もっとさらっと弾いてよかったんだな」と思ったり。自分なりの解釈がはっきりしてきたというのが、楽しいです。 21. これまでに「この人の音楽はすごい！」と衝撃を受けた音楽家はいますか？ 新倉 1人ではないんですが、あえて1人選ばせていただくなら、堤剛先生です。堤先生の音って、どの曲を聴いてもわかるんです。 私とは違う解釈で演奏されていても、ショパンやリヒャルト・シュトラウスのチェロ・ソナタ、ドヴォルザークの協奏曲、バッハなど、先生の説得力のある音が今でも耳に残っています。音色だけでなく、生徒としてではなく、常に一人の芸術家として接してくださったことも大きいです。 私が自分に自信をなくしていたときには「あなたの実力でここまで来ている」と背中を押してくださったり、クレズマー音楽など新しいことにも「素晴らしいですね」と耳を傾けてくださったり。学生時代には、クラシックではない民族音楽のCDをプレゼントしてくださったこともありました。 そういう意味でも、堤先生は私にとって特別な存在です。 ジャンルが違うと思いすぎずに新しい出会いを楽しむ 22. 今後一緒に演奏してみたい音楽家を一人挙げるとしたら、誰ですか？ 新倉 まだ存じ上げていない方との出会いがある気がしているので、そういう方との出会いを楽しみにしたいです。今この時点で、あえて1人挙げるとしたら、ダニエル・ゼペックさんです。 バーゼルに留学中に室内楽の授業を受けたのですが、一緒に演奏すると学べることがあると思います。ゼペックさんのベートーヴェンの音楽にも感銘を受けたので、一緒に室内楽を弾いてみたいです。 ダニエル・ゼペックによるベートーヴェン：ピアノ三重奏曲 23. ジャンルを越えた活動にも取り組まれていますが、新しい音楽に出会うときに大切にしていることは何ですか？ 新倉 結局、あまり「ジャンルが違う」と考えすぎないことだと思っています。自分が知らないことは、同じジャンルの中にもまだまだありますから。 新しい音楽に惹かれるときも、音楽そのものというより、「なぜこの魅力的な人は、この音楽を取り入れているんだろう」というところから興味を持つことが多いですね。 クレズマーなど東ヨーロッパの音楽に没頭していったのも、プロとアマチュアが一緒に演奏するバンドに入ったことがきっかけでした。音楽の響きはもちろんですが、そういう人たちに感動していることが多いんだと思います。 24. 今、音楽家として一番知りたいこと、探求したいことは何ですか？ 新倉 今回ベートーヴェンに取り組むことで、ベートーヴェンの知られざる一面をたくさん発見できました。なので、今回の12月3日の公演でも、きっと皆さまも「あ、そうなんだ」というところが見つかると思います。「そういう曲を書いていたんだ」とか、「そういう一面があるんだ」と。そういった意味で、残された曲に関しては、書かれた背景や作曲家の人となりを探求したいと思います。 うつむくベートーヴェンを気にかけてあげる新倉さん 25. これから、どんな音楽家になっていきたいですか？ 新倉 私は有名な国際コンクールに入賞しているわけでもないのですが、それでも第一線の皆さんと一緒に音を出させていただく機会に恵まれてきました。 なので、これからの若い方々が何か挫折したときに「あ、こういう音楽家もいた」と思っていただけるような、何か一つの例になれたらいいのかなと思っています。 いろいろなキャリアや肩書きがなくても、「自分なりの道があるよ」と思っていただける存在になりたいなと思っているので、それをキープ・ゴーイングでいきたいです。 新倉瞳に50の質問！〈後編〉新倉瞳の人となりは9月30日公開予定！ ポッドキャストの視聴はこちら 新倉瞳さんの出演情報 新倉瞳 × 南沢奈央 ベートーヴェンの小径 日時： 2026年12月3日（木）19：00開演 会場： サントリーホール ブルーローズ 曲目： 語りとともに綴るベートーヴェンの世界 ベートーヴェン／チェロ・ソナタ全曲 構成・脚本・演出： 新倉 瞳 出演： 新倉瞳（チェロ）、南沢奈央（語り）、横山瑠佳（ピアノ） スペシャルゲスト： 大萩 康司（ギター）、佐藤 芳明（アコーディオン）、大渕 愛子（フィドル）、渡辺 庸介（パーカッション） 詳しくはこちら

items.album: Amsterdam CS
items.excerpt: Anyone who’s spent time in large train stations late at night or early in the morning, before the commuter rush and the busy timetables begin, will have noticed that they are quite unique sonic environments. items.body: Anyone who’s spent time in large train stations late at night or early in the morning, before the commuter rush and the busy timetables begin, will have noticed that they are quite unique sonic environments. Vast and cavernous, open at both ends, with a proliferation of hard surfaces, and heavy machinery coming and going, central stations play host to a range of interesting acoustic phenomena: resonating eddies of wind, reverberant chugging of diesel and electric engines, and echoing clatters and clamours of all sorts. Amsterdam’s central station is a prime example of such an environment, and Cinema Perdu’s latest album is both named after and created in response to it. I’m not sure how many of the sounds on the album were derived from recordings made in the station, but I wouldn’t be surprised if it was 100%. For all I know, even the melancholic string-like chords and pitched tones used here and there could have been created through some sort of filtering of recorded sound; at any rate, they sound natural, part of the whole, rather than like add-ons. The liner notes state that the intention was not to accurately document or recreate the sounds of the station as they are heard directly, and apart from a few vague snatches of tannoy announcements, obvious sonic signifiers are avoided. Yet the impression created is very much one of a large train station: the hissing and ringing, the rumble and clatter, the quiet screeches, the billowing wind, and the general hubbub all seem instantly familiar. Often this seems to have as much to do with how the sounds change as much as their qualities at any one moment. The way the quiet ambient gleams and glimmers of the opening track breathe slowly in an out, as if we were listening to the respiration of the station, is but one example of this. Or perhaps that sense of familiarity stems from the music’s ability to evoke not only the sounds of a large central train station, but also the unique state of consciousness provoked by being in one. Regular visitors to such stations will know what I mean. There’s that sense of self-effacement, of merging with the environment; the intimate yet fleeting connections with hundreds of strangers; the endless waiting. On the album’s final track, rumble, ring, and clatter slowly build, before being overtaken by soft distortion. Hiss, clamour, and the billowing of wind create a slow-moving chaos. A glimmering chord slowly blossoms and sweeps the chaos away, like the rolling to a halt of the train that will take you home. Central train stations leave unique and indelible marks on the psyche, and “Amsterdam CS” traces those marks with skill and careful attentiveness. [bandcamp width=100% height=120 album=909022375 size=large bgcol=ffffff linkcol=0687f5 tracklist=false artwork=small track=3742585179] Cinema Perdu Moving Furniture Records

items.body: As Solid opens its gates, the music takes a single step forward before lifting off. A nascent, endlessly-echoing piano joins a grounded bass – the only part of the music that touches the ground at all – and an airy, washed-out progression enters, too, blossoming into something like a spring breeze. Swirling in light, yogurt-like textures and a playground spirit, sustaining itself and imbued with a fulfilling light, ‘Stones’ is the kindest of openers from Poland’s ambient duo, Bojanek & Michalowski. Things open up even more as the music begins to shape itself, resembling something like a mystical temple which reveals itself to only a select few. The electric guitar bends the atmosphere, shaping it by way of sonic architecture into a towering figure composed out of monolithic distortion and frayed melodies; a statue carving out the face of a God. The guitar rises slowly, gaining momentum as a rolling wave will as it approaches the shore before reaching the point of no return. It then breaks itself, collapsing like the dusty, sand-strewn stone that it is, an ancient rock that can no longer stand. This is where the track’s power lies: in its breaking. The distortion climbs, morphing into the indiscernible roaring of insectile static. It both washes and stains. The music rises up to titanic heights, and this is indicative of the track naming – monoliths, pillars, statues, sculptures. Even the greatest masterpiece must begin with a single stroke, and each journey must begin with a single step. Likewise, the opening note is the alpha and the omega, the first stone at the base of this perfectly-aligned pyramid; habitually repeating, but turning silence into sound and a Sahara drought into an overflowing oasis. At some level, the music is burning in a spell of torturous heat. Temperature-wise,Solid summons up the merciless spike of July or August, but it’s a dry heat, and not a humid, shirt-sticking suffocation. These pillars stand tall and proud. Even during the clashing of tribal drums, the music remains ambient and expansive enough, despite the dog-lead of repetition. But it acts both ways: one person may think of the bass as a restraint, but the bassline can also be a guide, a map back to camp via the predictability of its looping phrase. Popular music is built on anticipation, but it exists in ambient, too – usually in the form of traditional song, with examples being the vocal-heavy music of Julianna Barwick or Alicia Merz. This anticipation and release, this question and answer, can also be found in a loop, albeit lacking a proper resolution because of its repetition. Solid is energetic ambient, the kind that makes you feel alive instead of dosing it up on sleeping pills. Altitude is everywhere in the record. The flight attendant on ‘Figures’ asks passengers to put their seat belts on as the descent begins, but the reverb-soaked, cloud-wispy guitar chords are more like fluttering feathers or falling autumn leaves after the death of summer, while Jacaszek’s remix glides through cut-up pads and skimmers over soft and thin beats. Have a nice flight… www.ncoded.pl

items.body: By Nickolas Mohanna and Olli Aarni This April, Preservation have added two new releases to their catalogue – Mantis by Brooklyn-based musician Nickolas Mohanna and Muovia by Finland’s Olli Aarni. Nickolas Mohanna primarily works within synth modulation, but the New York musician adds a generous range of acoustic instruments to his music, nestling beside and behind the synths. Zithers, a bowed acoustic guitar, cymbals and bells are all featured, as are various objects found on the streets of New York. And New York City breathes through and out of the music; the synths are busy and hustling, every synth a new avenue or street to explore. They diverge at the end of the block, snaking around the corners. Traffic lights stop and start, pulsing in and out; walk, don’t walk. The afternoon stretches out before the music, its generally bright sound glinting in the weak sun, its sky muted and made pale by heavy, elephantine clouds. The synths start to take shape, and like a subway train they roll through the city at quicker (although they’re not exactly fierce or burning) speeds. When the other instruments enter the mix the synths drop out, leaving a swirling vortex behind. The other tones and timbres slowly inflate to fill the sparser vacuum. The synths hang around in the background, though, and they’re never gone for long. The incisive tones are capable of cutting and dividing up the music, but contrasting this, a series of smooth, muted notes breezes out of an afternoon jazz club, softening the track. This doesn’t last long, either. Mantis shifts between the experimental and the ephemerality of daily life, of transitory meditations on mindfulness that are sucked into the beating heart of a thriving, 24/7 city. Bleeding into one another, the tracks lightly rattle with sweeping, cymbal-led interludes and chiming bells reminiscent of far-away gongs specifically used for meditation and daily chanting. They tickle the side of the notes, barely grazing the music. ‘Silver Theme’ has a floating synth that climbs to a decent altitude. The night covers the city as a darker, crackling drone walks underneath the bridge of a tired piano, and the intermittent sounds by the side of the road cover the boroughs in black cloth. Muovia is the Finnish word for ‘plastic’. Similarly, his music has some degree of artificiality to it, lying there in its open, tranquil ocean among the tangled strands of seaweed and the pretty, colour-splashed coral. Inspired by old New Age music tapes, the music’s sensitive skin gently decays, tingling with soft sensations. The aquatic notes gently cascade, but the music’s been polluted by plastics and other debris. As a result, the sound is grainy and well-worn; it churns like the stomach of a whale after it has inadvertently swallowed something that shouldn’t be there. Still, the music is positive and the light tones ripple over the surface of the tape. Its New Age influence comes across beautifully; the music always refreshing the palette, always going into unexplored, exotic areas and discovering new species along the way. Its lighter, watery sound is more expansive, not timid in the slightest. The thirty minutes float serenely by. The decay is a second-by-second process; the same way that the body, after receiving life, slowly decays. Muovia isn’t in danger of becoming obsolete, of fading away. The crackles in the record’s skin wrinkle and tighten. It’s a noticeable creasing, but it’s just a part of the process of ageing, and the crackles actually give the record a feeling of authenticity that contrasts and contradicts the artificial nature of the plastic. Like the lovely, deep warmth of a needle resting on the groove of a vinyl record, this extra layer and its additional texture really is crucial to the overall weight and depth of the sound. Split into sides A and B, Muovia is a safe, serene cruise across totally tropical seas. www.preservation.com.au
